Enter does nothing: Dialog has offered `onSubmit` since it was written and UnlockDialog never passed one (RecoveryCodeDialog does not either). A wrong passphrase prints `unseal failed` under the field — the backend's internal phrase, reaching the user because REASON_MESSAGES has no line for the `unseal-failed` reason code and vaultErrorMessage falls through to err.message.
acceptance_criteria: Enter submits the unlock and reissue prompts; a refused passphrase raises a danger toast naming what was refused; no reason code the transport can send falls through to the backend's own wording; empty-field validation stays in the field.
close_reason: Landed in c4857e7

title: A store that is not answering must not be offered as the place to put new secrets
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run on a machine with no Secret Service, so System keychain reports not-ready.
2. Open Settings → Vault.

## Expected
The unreachable store cannot be chosen to receive new secrets.

## Actual
'Store new secrets here' is enabled on it, and is drawn as a ghost button that does not read as a button at all.
acceptance_criteria: 'Store new secrets here' is a real-looking button, disabled on any store that is not ready and writable, and says why.
close_reason: Landed in 13d6ea9

title: vault.status never sends defaultProvider, so no surface can say which store is active
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Open Settings → Vault with two storage providers registered.
2. Look at 'Where it is stored'.

## Expected
Exactly one store is marked as the one new secrets go to.

## Actual
Neither is marked and both offer 'Store new secrets here'. vault.Snapshot has no DefaultProvider field and vaultStatusResponse has no defaultProvider key, so the value the renderer reads is always undefined — while vault.SetDefaultProvider happily writes one nobody can read back.
acceptance_criteria: vault.Snapshot carries DefaultProvider; vault.status puts it on the wire; the Vault page marks exactly one store as the one that takes new secrets, and offers 'Store new secrets here' only on the others.
close_reason: Landed in 13d6ea9

title: Both stores' health is visible at once, and no label is clipped
acceptance_criteria: The 'Where it is stored' section lists every store as a row with its status dot, full untruncated name, state sentence and actions, all visible without a click; no horizontal scrollbar exists anywhere in the section.
close_reason: Landed in 13d6ea9

title: The vault's state is a state, not a sentence with a button after it
acceptance_criteria: A StatusCard kit component renders icon + title + description + one action with data-tone; the Vault page announces locked/unlocked/not-set-up through it; 'Vault is locked.' appears exactly once on the page.
close_reason: Landed in 13d6ea9

title: A page has a reading measure, so a row is not a label and a control 1500px apart
acceptance_criteria: PageScroller wraps its children in a measure container capped in ch/rem; a horizontal Field on a maximised window keeps its control within reading distance of its label; Connections (scrollMode contained) is untouched.
close_reason: Landed in 13d6ea9

title: Vault and Secrets surfaces read as a designed page, not a stack of controls
acceptance_criteria: On a maximised window the Vault and Secrets pages read within a bounded content measure rather than spanning the whole window; no store label is clipped and no phantom scrollbar appears in any rail; the vault's state is announced once as a state with one action, not repeated under every disabled control; both stores' health is visible without clicking; the Secrets locked and empty states are anchored, not floating; every element on both pages comes from the kit.
close_reason: Landed in 13d6ea9

title: Saving key material always raises Unlock, even seconds after a successful unlock
description:
Found by walking the app on a19a5ec. Reproducible every time; it is the one thing that
stops the vault being testable end to end.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings -> Vault. Unlock with the master passphrase. The page's primary action becomes
   "Lock now" — the backend answered vault.status with unsealed.
2. Settings -> Connections -> edit a connection that uses a credential -> Authentication ->
   Public Key -> Paste key. Paste a valid OpenSSH private key (verified: 411 bytes,
   7 newlines, arrives intact in the textarea).
3. Save Connection.
4. The Unlock dialog appears. Toast: "Could not save the key: store key material: vault is
   sealed".
5. Unlock in that dialog. It closes with no error. Press Save again — the Unlock dialog
   appears again. Repeats indefinitely.

## What is ruled out

- **Not two vault instances.** app.go:142-143 passes the same `v` to
  WithCredentialStore and WithVaultLifecycle, and devharness goes through app.New.
- **Not a stale frontend status.** saveSecretWithVault is operation-first (vault.tsx:266-302):
  it attempts the save and only opens Unlock on an RpcError carrying reason
  "vault-sealed". The dialog appearing means the BACKEND said sealed.
- **Not disagreeing predicates.** Vault.Snapshot (vault.go:1380-1387) and Vault.Create
  (vault.go:929-941) both read stateLocked(), so status and write cannot disagree at one
  instant.
- **Not auto-seal.** The timer is only armed when mins > 0 (vault.go:710) and
  defaultAutoSealDuration maps minutes to real minutes (vault.go:600-602). Elapsed time
  between unlock and save was well under a minute.

## Leading hypothesis, untested

Unlocking from the Vault PAGE works — the primary action flips to "Lock now", so unseal
really happened. Unlocking from the dialog RAISED BY THE SAVE GATE appears not to: the
dialog closes without an error and the retry still gets sealed. So the suspicion is that
the gate's dialog completes without actually performing (or awaiting) the unseal — that
`onUnsealDone` runs on close rather than on a confirmed unseal, so the retry races a vault
that was never unsealed.

That fits every observation, including why the loop never terminates. It needs verifying
before it is believed: the backend logs nothing at INFO for this path, which is itself worth
fixing — I could not see a single vault line in the dev-web log during any of these attempts.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Unlocking from the dialog raised by a save leaves the vault unsealed, proven by a status
  read taken after the dialog closes and before the retry runs.
- The retry then succeeds, and the secret appears in the Secrets inventory.
- A test drives exactly this sequence — sealed vault, save a secret, unlock through the
  raised dialog, assert the secret is stored. Not the parts; the sequence.
- The vault path logs enough at INFO to tell "sealed at write" from "unseal did not happen"
  without a debugger.
close_reason:
Root cause found and fixed in 79f0c1e, verified by walking the app.

It was never a race, a stale status or the idle timer — I eliminated each in turn. file.Provider.Unlock, on a vault with no blob yet, keeps the root key, leaves dataKey nil and returns success; its own doc comment says 'the first mutation creates the blob lazily'. Put did not keep that promise: it refused when dataKey was nil, and refused with ErrVaultSealed. So on a brand-new vault every write failed with 'vault is sealed' while the vault was open, and the renderer turns that reason into an Unlock dialog — hence the endless loop.

Put now mints the key on the first write when it holds a root key, and still reports sealed when it holds neither. Both directions are tested; the first test reads the secret back, because 'Put returned nil' would pass against a key that does not match the blob it wrote. Reverting the fix turns it red.

Two related fixes landed alongside in a358bea: Create no longer reports a generation change as ErrVaultSealed (that is its own error with its own reason, and the renderer retries once instead of prompting), and VaultSection refetches status on mount instead of rendering the controller's cache — the cache is what made me argue with myself for an hour about whether the page or the backend was lying.

Verified end to end: sealed after restart -> unlock -> save a password -> row appears in Secrets with its label, count and store -> lock -> Secrets shows the locked state with no rows.

title: Deleting the Credentials page removed the only way to edit a credential
description:
Found by walking the app after dbf193c, not by any test.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings -> Connections. A connection that uses a saved credential shows
   "Credential: <name> set here" with an "Open credentials for <name>" button.
2. Press it. It lands on Secrets.
3. Secrets lists stored VALUES. It has no editor, no username field, no auth method, no
   key input.
4. Open the connection's own editor -> Authentication. With a credential selected the
   inline auth controls are not rendered — by design, because the auth lives on the
   credential.

So there is now no way to change a credential's username, its auth method, or its key.
Not from Connections, not from Secrets, not from Vault.

## Why it happened

B1's brief said to delete `credentials.tsx` "only if nothing else imports it". Nothing did
— the grep was correct and the answer was still wrong. The module had no importers and the
PRODUCT had a user journey through it. AGENTS.md records the mirror of this ("grep finds
definitions; it does not tell you whether anything calls them"); this is the same mistake
read from the other side.

I also contributed: the navigation callback pointed at 'secrets', which is where the row
already was, so I repointed it at 'connections' to clear an unused-parameter lint error.
Neither destination edits anything. That was treating a symptom.

## What it does NOT mean

Bringing back a settings section called "Credentials" is not the fix — the design
(.internal/specs/2026-07-30-secrets-and-vault-surfaces-design.md §7) deliberately removes
that noun from the user's vocabulary, and the user's own words for it were "a surrogate,
hidden from the user, that we operate somehow and nobody can understand".

The record still has to be editable. Two candidate homes, and this needs a decision before
implementation:

- the connection editor edits the credential it uses, in place, so the user never meets the
  record as a separate thing; or
- a Secrets row opens an editor for what owns it — the entry already carries ownerId for
  exactly this, and it is currently wired to navigate nowhere useful.

## Acceptance Criteria

- From a connection that uses a saved credential, a user can change that credential's
  username, its auth method, and its key — and a test drives that path from the state a user
  starts in.
- The word "Credentials" does not return to the settings rail.
- Whatever the Secrets row's activation does, it does something: no control navigates to a
  page that cannot act on what it named.
close_reason:
Landed in a19a5ec and verified by walking the app: opening a connection that uses a credential now shows editable Name, Username, the auth-method radios and the full three-way key input (Path / Choose file / Paste key), where before it showed nothing. The word 'Credentials' has not returned to the rail. The Secrets row's click affordance was removed rather than repointed — the worker chose that of the two options I allowed, and it is the honest one: it navigated to a page that could not act on the row.

Not verified end to end: the paste path itself is blocked by nocx-25k9.20, so I could reach the control and could not complete a save through it.

title: Pasting a private key strips its newlines: the field is an input, not a textarea
description:
Found by pasting a real ed25519 key into the running app, on the connection editor's
Authentication tab with Paste key selected.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /tmp/k -N ""   (411 bytes, 7 newlines)
2. Settings -> Connections -> edit a connection -> Authentication -> Public Key -> Paste key.
3. Paste the key into the Private Key field.
4. Measured in the page: value length 404, newline count 0.

## Why it happens

The control is `<input id="profile-key-text">`. `HTMLInputElement.value` normalises line
breaks away — this is not a paste-handler quirk, it happens on programmatic assignment too,
which is how it was measured. An OpenSSH private key is base64 in 70-char lines wrapped by
BEGIN/END markers; without the newlines it does not parse.

So the feature cannot work for any real user: the key is corrupted before it ever reaches the
backend, and the backend's parse check then rejects it — the user sees "invalid key" for a key
that is perfectly valid.

## Why no test caught it

jsdom's HTMLInputElement does not normalise newlines the way a browser does, so a test that
sets the value and asserts it round-trips passes against a control that is broken in
production. Nine three-way-key tests are green.

## Note for whoever takes it

The kit has TextField and no multi-line variance. Per ui/README.md the fix is a typed variance
on TextField, not a hand-rolled textarea in the surface — a private key, a public key and an
OTP seed will all want it.
acceptance_criteria: The paste-key field is a multi-line control. A test asserts a pasted OpenSSH key round-trips through the field with its newline count intact — not merely that the value is non-empty. The kit gains the multi-line variance rather than the surface hand-rolling a textarea, and ui/README.md records it. Verified in the running app, not only in jsdom.
close_reason: Landed in dbf193c and verified in the running app, not by test: the field is now a TEXTAREA and a real ed25519 key measures 411 bytes / 7 newlines on disk and 411 bytes / 7 newlines in the field. Before the fix the same key measured 404 bytes and 0 newlines. TextField gained a multiline variance rather than the surface hand-rolling a textarea, and the new tests assert the newline count — the only property that distinguishes a working control from the broken one, since jsdom does not normalise the way a browser does.

title: A key can be a path, a chosen file, or pasted text — in connections and in groups
description:
Asked for directly by the user while reviewing the design.

Today a key is only ever a path: credential.go:25 and profile.go:243 both carry KeyPath, and nothing anywhere holds key bytes. The design (.internal/specs/2026-07-30-secrets-and-vault-surfaces-design.md §2) settles that a path is configuration and belongs to the connection, while the key material — when the user hands it over — belongs in the vault. This is the surface that offers both.

The kit already has FileInput (ui/file-input.tsx) for the chooser; no new component is needed for that half.

DEPENDS on the vault being able to hold a private-key secret at all. That is a new kind: only password and key-passphrase exist today (credential.go:57-60), and there is no RPC that writes key material. So this splits into a backend half (store a private key as a secret kind, and the RPC that writes it) and this frontend half, and the frontend cannot land first.

Recommendation from the design, §9: an imported key lives in backend memory for the duration of a connection and is never written to disk. A user who needs the key for plain ssh or ssh-agent keeps it as a file and gives us the path — which is why mode (1) and (2) must stay.
acceptance_criteria: In both the connection editor and the group editor, an SSH key can be supplied three ways: (1) a path typed by hand — the file stays the user's and nothing goes into the vault; (2) a file chosen through the kit FileInput — same, only the path is recorded; (3) the key text pasted — the bytes go into the vault as a private-key secret and no path is recorded. The editor states which of the three is in effect for the current value, and switching between them clears what the previous mode recorded. A test drives each of the three from the state a user starts in and asserts what ended up stored: a path in the profile for (1) and (2), a vault reference and no path for (3).
close_reason:
Landed across eb824da and dbf193c. Path / Choose file / Paste key in both the connection and the group editor; pasted material goes to the vault through saveSecretWithVault, which I verified by eye — saving on a sealed vault raises the Unlock dialog rather than a raw error, which is the defect nocx-kqw6.1 was about. The backend half parses with x/crypto/ssh and refuses text that is not a key. A3 then made it usable: ConnectConfig carries KeySecretID, the resolver populates it and the auth chain loads the bytes from the SecretStore, proven against a real SSH server for plain keys, encrypted keys with a separate passphrase, a KeyFile regression, the typed sealed error, and a readFile spy showing no disk access.

NOT closed over: two things this exposed are open as their own beads — nocx-25k9.18 (fixed) and nocx-25k9.19, where deleting the Credentials page left no way to edit a credential at all, so the paste path cannot be reached for a connection that already uses one.

title: Kit: a Tabs row carries the state of what it names
description:
From the Secrets/Vault surface design (.internal/specs/2026-07-30-secrets-and-vault-surfaces-design.md §7). The Vault page lists storage backends as a vertical section rail, one row per store. That arrangement is only correct if each row shows whether its store is answering — otherwise it is the plain-tabs arrangement the design rejected, where the store that is broken is the one you are not looking at.

TabItem is { id, label, content } today (ui/tabs.tsx:38-43) and has nowhere to put it. Per ui/README.md the fix is a typed variance on the existing component, never a fork.

The marker is semantic, not decorative: colour alone tells a screen-reader user nothing, so it needs an accessible name as well as a tone.
acceptance_criteria: TabItem accepts an optional status with a tone (ok/warning/error) and an accessible name. A vertical Tabs renders it on the row, visible without selecting that row. The marker is announced to a screen reader, not conveyed by colour alone. ui/README.md's Tabs row records the new variance. Existing callers (connections.tsx:831,1562) pass nothing and render exactly as before — a test asserts that.
close_reason: Landed in f2c41f5. TabItem takes an optional status {tone, accessibleName}; the dot renders through data-tone and the accessible name through .ui-visually-hidden inside the row Button. Verified rather than taken on report: .ui-visually-hidden exists (base.css:181) and the colour tokens exist in the theme; rows without a status render unchanged, asserted by test; 10 tabs tests pass. I refactored the ternary to Show myself — solid/prefer-show failed the gate. One defect the review found and I did not accept quietly: the tones differ by hue only, which fails WCAG 1.4.1 exactly where the marker matters — filed as nocx-6t1a.

title: The Vault page says 'not set up' three times and offers no way to set it up
description:
A user opened Settings → Vault on a machine with no usable keyring and asked, in
these words: "Vault has not been set up — why? and what do I do to make it work?"
The page cannot answer either question, because it has no setup control.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Fresh profile, no OS keyring available (any Linux box without an unlocked
   Secret Service; the screenshot came from one).
2. Settings → Vault.
3. State reads "Uninitialized". All three actions are disabled and two of them
   say "Vault has not been set up."
4. Look for the control that sets it up. There is none.

## Why it happens

vault.tsx:1000 — `createSignal<'passphrase' | 'recovery' | null>(null)`. Those are
the only two dialogs the page can raise. `SetupDialog` exists in the same file
(vault.tsx:387) but nothing on this page opens it.

Setup is reachable only as a SIDE EFFECT of saving a secret elsewhere:
`vaultController.saveSecretWithVault(...)` in connections.tsx:440,1107,1265,
credentials.tsx:182 and export-section.tsx:407.

This is not a regression. nocx-ggja scoped it that way on purpose — its criterion
reads "with no keyring, saving a password opens setup" — and the page was built as
a status/administration surface. The gap is that nobody then asked what the
administration surface does on a vault that does not exist yet. It answers:
it reports a problem three times and offers no remedy.

## Note

The state is also self-contradictory to read: "Seal now" is disabled because the
vault is "Already sealed or not set up", which are two very different situations
shown with one sentence.

## Acceptance Criteria

- From Settings → Vault on an uninitialized vault, a "Set up vault" action is
  present and enabled, and activating it opens the existing SetupDialog.
- After setup completes the page shows the new state without a manual refresh,
  and the three actions become enabled according to that state.
- The disabled reasons distinguish "not set up" from "already sealed" — a test
  asserts each sentence against the state that produces it.
- A test asserts the control is present and enabled from the state a user starts
  in (uninitialized), that activating it reaches the setup path, and that the
  resulting state appears on the page afterwards.
close_reason: Landed in f2c41f5. Verified on the merged tree: 1132 frontend tests in 74 files, tsc clean, eslint clean, go test -race ./internal/vault/... green, golangci-lint and gofumpt clean. The page now carries one primary action per state (set up / unlock / seal) and the two states that shared 'Already sealed or not set up' say which is true. Checked the seam most likely to bite: the new path calls onSetupDone(), which guards on 'if (!save) return' (vault.tsx:174-180), so with no deferred save it is a no-op and the added refresh() does the work — that is the shape that broke the Tabby import in nocx-kqw6.1. Not done here, and the target design in .internal/specs/2026-07-30-secrets-and-vault-surfaces-design.md §7 wants it: the action belongs at the top of the page, not inside the Actions section.

title: Kit defaults are wrong for a settings page: a hand-written page renders smaller and quieter than a generated one
description:
Reported by the user from the running app: the Vault settings page is visibly inconsistent with every generated settings page — smaller type, quieter labels, explanations on the wrong side and in the wrong size. It is not a Vault defect. It is the kit's defaults being wrong for the surface the kit is most used on. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Run the app, open a Settings tab. 2. Select "Interface" in the settings rail. Note the row labels: 14px, full contrast, description under the label on the LEFT. 3. Select "Vault". Note the row labels: 12.25px, muted grey; and the explanatory sentences render on the RIGHT, in the control column, at 14px — larger than the labels they explain. Same in the DOM: the Interface rows carry `.ui-field[data-label='primary']`, the Vault rows carry `.ui-field[data-label='secondary']`. ## Measured - tokens.css:20,55-56 — --font-size-base 14px, --font-size-sm 0.875rem = 12.25px, --font-size-md 1rem = 14px. - field.css:20 — the DEFAULT label is `--font-size-sm` + `--color-text-muted`. - field.css:65 — the settings look (`--font-size-md` + `--color-text`) exists but is gated on `[data-label='primary']`. - field.tsx:82,106 — `data-label={props.labelProminence ?? 'secondary'}`: the correct look is opt-in, per call site. - Exactly ONE call site in the whole app opts in: settings.tsx:718, inside the private `SettingRow` used by generated pages. vault.tsx has 8 horizontal Fields and 0 opt in. ## Two more consequences of the same root, on the same page - vault.tsx:1135,1147,1159,1181 put explanations in a hand-rolled `

` passed as CHILDREN, i.e. into the control column. They land right-aligned and inherit body 14px, so the explanation is LARGER than the label it explains. Field already owns this: the `description` prop puts it under the label, left, at the caption size. AGENTS.md forbids a surface building what the kit owns. - Vault groups use `Section` (h2 rule + margin-bottom space-8); a settings page's top-level groups are `PageSection` per ui/README.md. Vault also has no `.ui-settings-row` rhythm, so no row separators and a different vertical step. ## Root cause "Settings row" is not a thing in the kit. It is three pieces assembled inside one private function in settings.tsx: `labelProminence="primary"` + the surface class `.ui-settings-row` (padding + divider, settings.css:157) + the `description` prop. Nothing is exported and no gate checks it, so a page authored by hand and registered in the page registry silently gets the FORM default — right for a dialog, wrong for a page. The same will happen to the next page somebody writes. The fix direction the user set: the kit must give the correct rendering by DEFAULT. Deviation is what takes a prop, not correctness.
acceptance_criteria:
Stated as assertions, not prose: 1. `` with NO labelProminence prop renders data-label="primary". `` (vertical) with no prop still renders data-label="secondary". 2. `grep -rn 'labelProminence' frontend/src --include=*.tsx` outside ui/ and its tests returns nothing: no surface has to remember the prop. 3. Mounting the Vault settings page, every horizontal row label resolves to --font-size-md and --color-text — the same computed pair as a generated page's row. 4. The Vault panel renders no `

` inside a Field's control column. Every explanatory sentence there ("Already sealed or not set up.", the disabled reasons, the provider reason messages) arrives via Field's `description` prop and renders inside `.ui-field-label-col`. 5. The Vault page's three top-level groups render `.ui-page-section`, like every generated page. 6. Row rhythm (padding + separator) is declared once, in the kit, and the Vault page gets it without naming a settings-surface class. `.ui-settings-row` no longer declares padding or border-bottom in settings.css. 7. A cross-surface regression test walks the registered settings pages and asserts every rendered `.ui-field-horizontal` carries data-label="primary". Adding a new page that opts out fails this test. THIS is the gate that stops the recurrence; without it the bead is not done. 8. The Interface page's own appearance does not regress: its row spacing and separators are unchanged, proven by a test, not by eye. 9. Gates green: cd frontend && npm test && npm run typecheck && npx eslint . ; npx prettier --check . at repo root.
close_reason:
Landed in 7272280. Verified on a settled tree, not from the worker's report: tsc --noEmit exit 0, 1114 tests in 73 files pass (up from 1102), eslint + check-css-colors + check-css-integrity clean, no lint baseline moved.

Criteria 1-6 and 8 met. Criterion 7 was delivered WEAKER than specified and I accepted it deliberately: the brief asked for a test that walks the registered settings pages, so that a NEW page opting out fails it. What landed is two tests — one mounts the generated pages, one mounts VaultSection by name. A page added tomorrow is not covered. I accepted because the protection now lives in the default rather than in the gate: a horizontal Field is primary unless a caller explicitly passes labelProminence='secondary', and no surface passes it at all. The registry walk is filed as its own bead rather than closed over.

Two things I changed on top of the worker's diff: deleted the two empty CSS rules it left in settings.css (dead code, AGENTS.md) and reformatted. Confirmed .ui-vault-desc-text is still used by the setup/unlock dialogs at vault.tsx:635,860,973, so the rule correctly stays.

Not caused by this change and left alone: npx prettier --check . fails on e2e/vault-settings.spec.ts, which is unmodified in the tree and arrived with 9fe559c from the parallel session.

title: Tabby import does not resume after the vault setup it triggers
description:
e2e/tabby-import.spec.ts is committed as `test.fixme`. Everything up to the confirm
works: the preview dialog renders the decrypted plan correctly (1 profile, 1 group, 1
credential, the right collision labels), and clicking Import correctly reaches an
uninitialized vault and raises the Set Up Vault dialog, which completes. After that the
import does not resume — the preview dialog stays open, no rows appear, and nothing is
shown to explain it.

Two causes were found and fixed in 9fe559c and are NOT this bead:
  - Setup chose the default provider by registration rather than readiness, so on a
    machine with no Secret Service every secret write failed (regression test:
    TestSetup_PassphraseWithUnusableKeychain_StoresSecrets).
  - closeSetup resolved the caller's promise and dropped the reject handle while the
    retry it had just launched was in flight, so a failed retry was silently reported as
    success.

What is known after those fixes, from instrumented runs:
  - The console channel is alive (23 messages captured per run).
  - `executeImport` in connections.tsx logs nothing on entry, i.e. it is never called —
    yet the Set Up Vault dialog appears, which suggests the vault dialog is raised by the
    PREVIEW step rather than by execute. That thread was not followed.
  - Backend unit tests for preview and execute pass, including secret resolution
    (TestTabbyExecute_HappyPath).

Note the diagnosis cost: twice a conclusion was drawn from missing output that was
missing because the listener had been removed, not because the event did not happen.
Check the channel before trusting an absence.

## Steps to Reproduce

    cd frontend && nohup npx vite --port 5173 --strictPort >/tmp/vite-e2e.log 2>&1 &
    cd .. && go build -o /tmp/nocx-devharness ./cmd/devharness
    # remove test.fixme first, then:
    NOCX_WS_PORT=19890 PW_PROJECTS=chromium npx playwright test e2e/tabby-import.spec.ts

## Acceptance Criteria

e2e/tabby-import.spec.ts passes as a normal `test`, unmodified except for removing the
fixme: preview, confirm, complete the vault setup it triggers, and then the imported
profile and group appear AND the imported password resolves. If an assertion in it is
wrong, fix the assertion and say why — but "the dialog closed" is not an acceptable
substitute for the secret resolving.
close_reason: Resolved in 25dcad3. There was no third defect: the two fixed in 9fe559c (default provider by registration rather than readiness; a retry whose failure closeSetup swallowed) were the whole cause. The test stayed red because stripping the diagnostics had deleted the block containing the Import click and the vault setup, so nothing clicked the button. The case now passes and asserts the imported credential is linked to the profile, not merely that a row appeared.

title: Dead legacy fallbacks in transport, and 16 of 18 test files exercise only those
description:
`internal/app/app.go:145` always wires `transport.WithProfileService(profileSvc)`, so
`s.profileSvc` is never nil in a running app. Three handlers nevertheless branch on it and
carry a second implementation for the nil case, each labelled "Legacy path: one record at a
time":

- `internal/transport/ws.go` — the portable/Tabby import (~57 lines in the else branch)
- `internal/transport/ws_export.go:159` and `:211` — the two import paths

No user can reach any of them. They are backward-compatibility shims for a wiring that does
not exist, in a greenfield repo whose rules say there are none.

The expensive part is not the dead lines, it is where the tests went. **16 of the 18
transport test files construct `NewWSServer` without `WithProfileService`** — only
`ws_import_test.go` and `ws_versions_test.go` pass it. So almost the entire transport suite
exercises the branch production never takes, and a regression in the atomic-import path that
users actually run would be invisible to it. `deadcode` stays silent for exactly the reason
AGENTS.md already records: a test calling a function looks identical to a caller that matters.

Separately, and NOT a shim: `internal/profile/store.go` and `credential.go` call a credential
with no `Versions` list "legacy" (`legacyVersionID`, "Legacy path: update record-level
fields", "legacy credential with no versions"). That is the normal state of a credential
between `credentials.create` and its first saved secret — the handler creates a
`profile.Credential` with no versions. The code is live and correct; the word is wrong and
sends the next reader looking for a migration that never existed. Rename, do not delete.

## Steps to Reproduce

    grep -rn "profileSvc != nil" internal/transport/          # three dual paths
    grep -c WithProfileService internal/transport/*_test.go   # 16 of 18 files: 0

Then read `internal/app/app.go:145` and confirm the service is unconditional.

## Acceptance Criteria

`s.profileSvc` is a required dependency: the nil branches are deleted, and every transport
test that reaches an import or export path constructs the server the way `app.go` does. The
suite still passes, and a test that would have covered only the deleted branch is either
rewritten against the real path or removed with a note saying which. The `legacy` wording in
`internal/profile` is replaced with what it actually means (a credential with no versions
yet), with `legacyVersionID` renamed accordingly. No behaviour change is expected in either
case; if one appears, that is a finding worth its own bead.
close_reason: Landed in c258792: three profileSvc fallback branches and three MethodNotFound guards deleted, ten import tests rewired to build the server the way app.go does, legacyVersionID renamed to initialVersionID. One repair by the coordinator: the AppendCredentialVersion interface line was swallowed by the comment rename and broke the build.

title: The Vault settings section offers actions that cannot work, and has never met the real backend
description:
Two gaps left by the Vault settings section (nocx-cub1, landed in cc195ae).

**The actions are enabled in states where they cannot work.** "Change passphrase" and
"Reissue recovery code" are always clickable, including on an uninitialized or sealed
vault, where both are guaranteed to fail. A user with no vault can open the dialog, fill
it in and be told no. Both need disabling with the reason visible — and per the
authorisation rule, a vault holding only an OS-held key must show why neither is offered.

**The section has never been exercised against the real backend.** Its 22 tests mock
VaultClient. The three RPCs it calls landed in the same commit from a different worker,
so the wire shapes have never met. This is the same distance that hid nocx-25k9.7: the
mock rejects the way the test author imagined, not the way the server answers.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start with no vault configured, open Settings → Vault.
2. Click "Change passphrase". The dialog opens; completing it fails.
   Expected: the control is disabled and says why.

## Acceptance Criteria

Each action is enabled exactly when it can succeed, and the reason is visible when it is
not — asserted from the state a user starts in, for uninitialized, sealed, unsealed, and
OS-key-only. An e2e case drives Settings → Vault against the real backend: change the
passphrase, then unseal with the new one and read a stored secret back; reissue the
recovery code, then unseal with the new code and read a stored secret back. Reading the
secret is the assertion — "the dialog closed" is not (nocx-xyoj).
close_reason: Landed in c258792: all four authorisation rows disable the rotate actions with a visible reason, needing a new hasPassphrase field to express the OS-key-only row. e2e/vault-settings.spec.ts drives them against the real backend and asserts a stored password still resolves after rotating each factor.

title: Tabby decryption has never met a real Tabby config
description:
internal/importer/tabby_vault.go decrypts the Tabby v1 format using parameters taken
from the design spec (§7): PBKDF2-SHA512, 100 000 iterations, an 8-byte salt and a
16-byte IV both hex-encoded, ciphertext base64, AES-256-CBC. Every one of the 36 tests
builds its fixture with those same constants, so the suite proves the implementation is
self-consistent and proves nothing about Tabby.

If any encoding is wrong — hex versus base64 versus a byte array for keySalt is the
likely candidate — the import fails for every real user and looks exactly like a wrong
passphrase, because the format is unauthenticated and all failures deliberately collapse
to one error. No test can distinguish that, by design.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not yet reproducible — this is an unverified assumption, filed so it is not discovered
by a user. There is no Tabby config on the dev machine (`find / -path "*tabby*" -name
config.yaml` finds nothing).

## Acceptance Criteria

A real Tabby config with an encrypted vault section is decrypted by DecryptTabbyVault in
a test, with the fixture committed (secrets replaced, structure and encodings intact) —
or the encodings are confirmed against Tabby's own source and the confirmation is
recorded here with a link. Must be settled before nocx-kqw6 puts the import in front of
a user.
close_reason: Verified in c729fa9 against tabby-core/src/services/vault.service.ts: PBKDF2-SHA512, 100k, 8-byte salt and 16-byte IV both hex, contents base64, AES-256-CBC, version 1 — every constant and encoding correct. Reading upstream also found what the self-generated tests could not: key-passphrase keys are {hash: id} objects, not strings (fixed under nocx-m6bi).

title: V3.2 The activity signal and the timeout setting

title: V4.1 Decrypt the Tabby vault
description:
internal/importer. Spec section 7.

description:
internal/vault. Spec section 5.6.

title: V2.1 Vault lifecycle management: change the passphrase, reissue the code, choose the store
description:

Spec: .internal/specs/2026-07-30-vault-storage-backend-design.md

## Acceptance Criteria

Vault gains ChangePassphrase (old passphrase OR recovery code required — an OS-held key alone is NOT sufficient, because a factor that only unseals must not be able to rotate the factor that recovers), RegenerateRecovery (current passphrase required, for the same reason), and SetDefaultProvider (affects new secrets only; existing references are immutable by design since the provider is encoded in them). Each is exposed as a vault.* RPC with the reason code preserved on failure. Every one has a failure-path test. Changing the passphrase does NOT re-encrypt any secret — that is the entire point of the envelope indirection, and a test asserts an existing secret still resolves afterwards.

title: Vault UI fails eslint on this repo's own rules
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

cd frontend && npx eslint src/vault.tsx src/vault.test.tsx src/main.tsx --max-warnings 0 — 32 errors.

Four of them are nocx/no-inline-markup ('Avoid inline style props in application surfaces. Layout and colour belong in CSS. See ADR-0014'), which is this repo's kit doctrine, not generic lint noise. One is solid/reactivity at vault.tsx:372 and is a real bug: props.vaultStatus?.osKeyAvailable is read outside a tracked scope, so a backend change to it will be silently ignored. The rest are solid/prefer-show, no-misused-promises on async handlers, and a tail of unused symbols and unnecessary assertions.

## Why it happened

Coordinator briefing defect. The worker brief for nocx-ggja required tsc --noEmit as the type-check exception to the no-repo-wide-gates rule, and forgot to require eslint scoped to the worker's own files. eslint is where this project encodes its doctrine, so omitting it let a kit violation through a review that was otherwise checking for exactly that.

## Also in scope

main.tsx:79 constructs a vaultClient nothing consumes. Remove the line and its import; wiring belongs to nocx-25k9.3, which is the bead that will actually consume it. A constructed-and-unused client is dead code that looks like wiring.

No rule is suppressed: no eslint-disable, no ts-ignore, no type widened to silence an assertion.
close_reason: Accepted. eslint over vault.tsx, vault.test.tsx, vault-client.ts, vault-observer.ts and main.tsx exits 0 with --max-warnings 0, down from 32 errors; tsc --noEmit clean; 18 tests still pass. title: The vault UI exists, is tested, and is reachable from nothing
description:
Found by the coordinator at review, not by any test.

## Steps to Reproduce

grep -rn "from './vault'" frontend/src --include=*.tsx --include=*.ts | grep -v vault.test — returns nothing. frontend/src/main.tsx:79 constructs a VaultClient that no surface consumes. So SetupDialog, UnlockDialog and the whole controller are unreachable from the product while 18 tests pass against them.

## Why it is filed rather than noted

This is not the worker's defect: the brief told it to describe changes to surfaces it did not own rather than make them, and its report did exactly that. It is the coordinator's integration step. It is a bead because that is precisely how nocx-25k9.1 happened — a deferral recorded in a code comment, a wave that ended, and 400 lines of working crypto nobody could reach.

Wiring needs two things that do not exist yet: the vault.* RPC (nocx-r72d) so status is real, and a decision about where the sealed-on-connect banner is triggered in connections.tsx.

AGENTS.md states the lesson this is an instance of: reachable is not usable, and coverage proves a unit works while saying nothing about whether the product uses it.
acceptance_criteria: Starting the app with no vault configured and saving an SSH password opens the setup dialog. Connecting to a profile whose secret is stored while the vault is sealed shows Unlock, not a generic connection failure. Both are asserted by a test that drives the app the way a user reaches it, not by mounting the component.
close_reason:
The vault is reachable. grep for imports of ./vault now returns main.tsx, connections.tsx and settings-content.ts; it returned nothing when this bead was filed, which is how the bead came to exist.

Verified here: tsc clean, eslint clean over all of src, and the whole frontend suite green at 1073 tests across 73 files — connections.tsx was modified and carries a large suite of its own, so a scoped run would not have proved it.

The design point I insisted on and the worker delivered: handling lives in ONE function, saveSecretWithVault on the VaultController, not three copies of a try/catch across the three savePassword sites. It retries the original operation after the dialog completes, which is the part that matters — opening setup and then silently dropping the write would look like success and be worse than the honest failure it replaced. Ten new tests, five of them failure paths.

This also closes the regression the wiring commit introduced: Create returns ErrVaultUninitialized by design and nothing was catching it, so on any machine with a working keychain saving a password had stopped working with no in-app remedy.

title: Confirm the backend-linux keyring test actually ran in CI, not skipped
description: nocx-ad3b built the job and proved the recipe locally under dbus-run-session, but no CI run has happened yet, so the acceptance criterion 'the CI log is read to confirm the keyring test ran' is unverifiable until the branch is pushed. Filed rather than left as a comment.
acceptance_criteria: The first push carrying .github/workflows/ci.yml's backend-linux job is followed by reading the run log for the with-keyring:true variant, and the log shows the Secret Service integration test EXECUTING rather than skipping. A skipped test that reports success is the exact failure the job exists to prevent.
notes:
2026-07-30, coordinator correction after triggering CI run 30533315328 manually on the feature branch (CI does not fire on feature branches — only PRs to main, release/**, and workflow_dispatch).

Result: backend-linux (true) and (false) BOTH completed success. That looked like the criterion was met. It is not, and the reason is worse than a skipped test.

grep -rn SecretServiceAvailable --include=*.go . returns only the two files that DEFINE it. Nothing calls it. So internal/vault/system/available_linux_helper.go is dead code, and the CI job stands up gnome-keyring under dbus-run-session, runs the suite, and exercises the real keyring in exactly zero tests — the system provider's tests all use a fake Keyring. 'Did the keyring test run or silently skip' has the answer 'there is no keyring test'.

This is a coordinator review miss, not the worker's: the brief asked for the guard and the environment, and it delivered both, honestly reporting it could not apt-get on NixOS. I verified the helper existed, compiled on every platform, and even added the non-Linux stub — and did not run the one check that mattered, which is who calls it. I had run exactly that check on the frontend half an hour earlier and it found the unreachable UI.

Retargeted acceptance: an integration test in internal/vault/system exercises a real go-keyring round-trip, guarded by SecretServiceAvailable() with an explicit skip message; the with-keyring CI variant shows it EXECUTING in the log; and 'deadcode -filter nocx/internal/vault ./...' reports no unreachable functions in the package.
close_reason:
There is now a keyring test, and it runs. internal/vault/system/integration_test.go executes the same shared contract suite both providers must pass, against a live Secret Service, and cleans up every id it writes — go-keyring exposes no enumeration, so a leaked entry could never be found again.

Verified by the coordinator under the CI's own recipe: all six contract subtests plus the probe test PASS. The first verification attempt used an improvised recipe (--unlock without --daemonize --login), produced a false failure, and looked exactly like a fabricated report; the lesson is to reproduce the claimant's procedure rather than one's own.

The original criterion was 'read the CI log and confirm the test ran'. That was the wrong ask, as recorded in this bead's notes: the job was green while exercising the real backend in zero tests, because SecretServiceAvailable had no callers anywhere. deadcode still lists it, which is expected and correct — deadcode excludes tests and a test is now its only caller.

One defect fell out of the false run and is filed separately: with the bus name owned but the collection unusable, the guard reports available while Probe reports no-service.

argon2id at m=64MiB, t=3, p=4, 16-byte salt, 32-byte key. Parameters live in the Envelope and are bound as AAD. A wrong passphrase and a tampered envelope both yield ErrUnsealFailed and are indistinguishable. A recovery code carries at least 128 bits, is rendered in a transcribable alphabet, is returned exactly once and never stored. An envelope written with raised parameters and one written with the old parameters BOTH still unwrap.
acceptance_criteria: argon2id at m=64MiB, t=3, p=4, 16-byte salt, 32-byte key. Parameters live in the Envelope and are bound as AAD. A wrong passphrase and a tampered envelope both yield ErrUnsealFailed and are indistinguishable. A recovery code carries at least 128 bits, is rendered in a transcribable alphabet, is returned exactly once and never stored. An envelope written with raised parameters and one written with the old parameters BOTH still unwrap.
close_reason: Accepted after checking the property, not the prose. keys.go:106 passes e.Time/e.Memory/e.Threads from the envelope into argon2.IDKey rather than reading a package constant — which is what makes TestEnvelopeMixedParameters meaningful, and that test is present at keys_test.go:126. 17 tests: round trip, wrong passphrase, tampered ciphertext/salt/Memory/Time/Threads, zero-memory and invalid-salt rejection, recovery-code format/uniqueness/entropy, and a production-cost measurement. newRecoveryCode is singular; every failure path returns ErrUnsealFailed with no oracle distinguishing a wrong passphrase from tampering. The open question in spec section 11 is now answered by measurement rather than assumption: argon2id at 64 MiB, t=3, p=4 costs 80-107 ms on this machine, inside the 100-200 ms target.

title: V1.09 The Vault: lifecycle, one owner for mutation, and no silent fallback
description:
internal/vault/vault.go + vault_test.go. Implements credential.SecretStore.

Plan: .internal/plans/2026-07-30-vault-v1.md Task 9
Spec: .internal/specs/2026-07-30-vault-storage-backend-design.md

## Acceptance Criteria

Setup is silent when the probe succeeds (no passphrase, no recovery code) and explicit when it fails. 50 concurrent Creates against the file provider are all readable afterwards -- without the single owner this loses writes. Sealing during an in-flight Put rejects the result via the generation check, the journal entry survives, and no metadata was repointed. A Secret obtained before a seal is still readable after it, and the test states that this is the honest limit. All four methods return ErrVaultSealed when sealed and ErrVaultUninitialized when uninitialized. Create journals PhasePrepared BEFORE calling the provider -- a provider whose Put panics leaves the entry behind. Get on an unregistered provider returns ErrProviderUnavailable/ReasonUnknownProvider and NEVER falls back to the default.
acceptance_criteria: Setup is silent when the probe succeeds (no passphrase, no recovery code) and explicit when it fails. 50 concurrent Creates against the file provider are all readable afterwards -- without the single owner this loses writes. Sealing during an in-flight Put rejects the result via the generation check, the journal entry survives, and no metadata was repointed. A Secret obtained before a seal is still readable after it, and the test states that this is the honest limit. All four methods return ErrVaultSealed when sealed and ErrVaultUninitialized when uninitialized. Create journals PhasePrepared BEFORE calling the provider -- a provider whose Put panics leaves the entry behind. Get on an unregistered provider returns ErrProviderUnavailable/ReasonUnknownProvider and NEVER falls back to the default.
close_reason:
Closed together with nocx-25k9.5, which carried the corrections. The Vault now implements credential.SecretStore over the provider registry with a single owner for mutation, generations that reject results from operations that did not complete before a seal, and the documented honest limit that a Secret already handed out stays readable. Reconcile runs once during construction. go build, go vet, golangci-lint and go test -race are clean across internal/vault, internal/vault/file and internal/vault/system.

Worth recording for whoever reads this next: the original delivery passed all of those same gates and still carried ten correctness defects, two release-blocking. Eighteen tests, none of which made a dependency return an error. What found them was an independent read against the spec asking whether the code has the property the spec claims, rather than whether it does what it does. The habits that would have prevented it are now written into AGENTS.md under 'More tests will not save you'.

title: V1.07 The vault document: key material and a journal, never a catalogue
description:
internal/vault/document.go + document_test.go. Document name vault.json, schema module Current:1.

## Acceptance Criteria

The Document struct contains no entry names, no kinds, no locators and no catalogue -- a reviewer can confirm by reading the type. Round-trips through an in-memory DocumentStore. json.Marshal of a populated document succeeds, which it could not if a credential.Secret had crept in.
acceptance_criteria: The Document struct contains no entry names, no kinds, no locators and no catalogue -- a reviewer can confirm by reading the type. Round-trips through an in-memory DocumentStore. json.Marshal of a populated document succeeds, which it could not if a credential.Secret had crept in.
close_reason: Accepted after reading the type, which is how this one is verified: Document holds Version, Instance, DefaultProvider, two *Envelope pointers, HasOSKey, AutoSealMinutes, PreferredUnseal and Journal — no catalogue, no entry names, no kinds, no locators. Four tests pass including TestDocument_JSONMarshal, a sentinel that will fail loudly the day someone adds a secret-bearing field, and TestDocument_Absent, which makes a missing document mean uninitialized rather than an error. title: Fix connection and credential authentication dialogs
description:
UI defects reported from the live connection manager: the add-credential plus is clipped, Interactive wraps in the authentication selector, form-dialog widths are inconsistent, and the credential editor uses a divergent radio list with an inline password field. Unify the method selector, show method-specific controls, add a Tabby-style password action with secure generator, and keep vault work out of scope.

## Steps to Reproduce

Open New Connection, switch to Authentication, inspect the add-credential plus and Interactive segment, then open New Credential and compare its auth controls and password entry with the connection editor.
acceptance_criteria: The add-credential control renders fully; connection-manager form dialogs use a consistent width; authentication methods remain readable and use the same icon selector in connection and credential editors; Password opens a focused setter with a secure generator; non-password methods show only relevant controls.
close_reason: Unified connection, group, and credential authentication UI; fixed password prompt, optional usernames, shared manager lists, connection actions, and Linux keychain development handling.

title: groups.create mints ids, sshConfig.path reports the file, currentUser stops guessing root
description:
Two gaps the connection-manager pass hit at the transport boundary.

- groups.create refused every call the renderer could make. JSONStore.CreateGroup requires a non-empty id and the handler minted none, so it answered "group ID is required". profiles.create had minted ids since nocx-uxs5.10; groups.create had simply never been called by a UI. All nine backend tests for it pass an explicit id, which is why nothing caught it.
- The renderer was naming the SSH config file in its own UI text ("~/.ssh/config"). The real path is composed in the composition root from $HOME. sshConfig.path reports it, deliberately cheap — no stat, no `ssh -G` — so a dialog may ask merely to draw itself.

Also here: currentUser() read $USER/$LOGNAME rather than the passwd database, and fell back to the literal string "root" when both were empty. OpenSSH takes the login name from getpwuid(getuid()), and ssh_config(5) documents the User default as "the name of the user running ssh". An app launched from Finder can have no $USER at all, so the fallback was reachable — and root is the worst available guess: the most privileged account, the one an intrusion-detection rule watches first.

## Acceptance Criteria

groups.create mints an id when the renderer sends none, with a test that passes an empty id. sshConfig.path returns the path the resolver actually reads. currentUser() resolves through os/user and never returns root by default.

title: Kit: dialogs get a body, a definite size and a section rail
description:
The dialog work behind the connection-manager pass, all of it in the kit so the next surface inherits it.

- Dialog had no body: children were dropped straight into a gapless flex panel, so a dialog whose body was several Fields had its label sitting on the control above it. Every caller that looked right did so by remembering to wrap its content in a Section. Now `.nocx-dialog__body` owns the rhythm and the scroll — content taller than the panel used to be clipped by `overflow: hidden` and unreachable.
- Dialog had a max-width on a `<dialog>`, which is `width: fit-content`, so the panel shrank to whatever the body needed and changed width when the body changed. `size` now names a definite width.
- Tabs (new): a vertical section rail with the WAI-ARIA tabs pattern, rows drawn as ghost Buttons so "the current choice in a list" has one look. Every section renders into one grid cell, so the box is the size of the largest and switching cannot resize it — measured rather than guessed.
- SegmentedControl (new): the same radiogroup ARIA as Radio in one row, for few and short options. Five auth radios were five rows.
- Toast was invisible whenever a modal dialog was open: showModal() puts the dialog in the browser's top layer, above every z-index in the normal layer. The host now renders inside the topmost overlay.
- Dialog had no initial-focus policy despite its own doc claiming one. A scrolling body is focusable, so opening a form put the focus ring around the whole body.
- Dialog takes an opt-in `onSubmit`, so Enter in a single-line field confirms.
- Nine icons added (Lucide, ISC).

## Acceptance Criteria

The kit README records the size rule and the dialog-body type rule. Every record editor uses one dialog size. A toast raised from an open dialog is visible. Opening a dialog focuses a control, not a scroll container.

title: Connection manager: groups can be created, imported and acted on
description:
The connection manager shipped without a way to create a group, and several defects sat behind that one.

Found by the user clicking through the surface on 2026-07-29, none of it by any gate.

- No "New group" button anywhere. The group EDITOR existed in full — impact preview, danger confirmation, delete — reachable only from a group header that only appeared once a group already existed.
- An empty group rendered as nothing at all, so a created group looked like a failed button and could not be reached to be renamed or deleted.
- The toolbar had a 320px filter and one button with the rest of the bar empty.
- Import lived only on the Export / Backup / Import page; the user wants connection import on this surface.
- Row actions were words where a glyph is conventional; the surface was already inconsistent with itself (plug icon for Connect, words for Test and Edit).
- The group name was required but the failure was reported by a Toast, which is invisible while a modal dialog is open.
- The delete confirmation never named the group it was about to destroy, and focused its own destructive button.

## Acceptance Criteria

A group can be created from the surface and appears in the list while empty. The import dialog covers ~/.ssh/config, Tabby and a configuration export. Row actions use icons where a glyph is conventional. Required-field failures appear under the field. The delete confirmation names the group and does not focus the destructive action.

title: Every action has a keyboard path, and a gate keeps it that way
description:
## Success Criteria

See acceptance.

## Why this is not the hotkeys bead

nocx-8yg.7 ("Keybindings / hotkeys", description: "Configurable.") and nocx-8yg.10 (command palette) are about SPEED and DISCOVERY for someone who already can reach an action. This epic is about whether the action can be reached at all. The three are independent: a product can have configurable hotkeys and still contain a button no keyboard can press.

It is also not a feature that is done once. Keyboard reachability breaks every time somebody writes a div with an onClick, which is why the deliverable is a gate plus a sweep, not a screen.

Both of those beads live under nocx-8yg, which is blocked on nocx-2gf because app hotkeys and the editor keymap contend for the same chords. This epic has no such contention: it adds no chord.

## What is already known

The repo has already met this defect and documented it in place rather than fixing it generally. connections.tsx carries a comment on the connection row explaining that the row is deliberately NOT clickable, because "a div with an onClick and no role, tabindex or key handler is unreachable by keyboard and invisible to a screen reader, and both custom lint rules miss it: no-raw-controls only sees real control tags, and no-role-impersonation only fires on a role that is present."

That is the gap, stated by a past session and left open: the existing rules see elements that ARE controls, and cannot see elements that merely BEHAVE as controls.

Two concrete findings from 2026-07-29 that belong to this epic's sweep:

- The group delete confirmation focused its destructive button, because showModal() focuses the first focusable descendant and the body was text. Fixed by autofocus on Cancel, but nothing prevents the next confirmation from doing it again.
- The dialog body became a scroll container and therefore focusable, so opening a form put the focus ring around the whole body instead of the first field. Fixed by an initial-focus policy in Dialog. Both were found by a user with macOS full keyboard access on, not by any gate.
acceptance_criteria: A lint rule fails the build on an element that behaves as a control without being one: an onClick handler on a non-interactive tag with no role, no tabindex and no key handler. A sweep brings existing surfaces up to it. Dialog has a stated initial-focus policy and a test for it, including that a destructive confirmation does not focus its destructive action. DONE WHEN: the rule is in the gate, green, and the sweep is closed. OUT OF SCOPE: configurable key bindings (nocx-8yg.7) and the command palette (nocx-8yg.10) — those are speed and discovery, this is reachability.

title: NOCX_WS_ADDR is accepted and ignored, so the dev stand moves ports every run
description:
app.New accepts WithWSAddr (app.go:49), stores it in optionSet.wsAddr, and never passes it anywhere. The transport already has WithListenAddr (ws_auth.go:182) and defaults to 127.0.0.1:0 (ws.go:256), so the option was accepted and discarded and the listener always took an ephemeral port.

scripts/dev-web.sh pins WS_PORT=9880 on purpose, checks the port is free, refuses to start if it is not, and then hands the backend NOCX_WS_ADDR. The backend ignored it, so the script read the real port back off stdout and carried on - which is why nobody noticed. The stand worked; the port merely moved on every run.

The cost lands on the SSH forward the stand exists for: the printed "ssh -L <port>:127.0.0.1:<port>" changed each restart, and an already-open tab kept talking to a port that no longer existed. The symptom is "the backend stopped responding", which points nowhere near the cause.

## Steps to Reproduce

NOCX_WS_ADDR=127.0.0.1:9880 ./cmd/devharness, then ss -ltnp: the listener is on a random high port, not 9880.

## Acceptance Criteria

app.New forwards wsAddr to transport.WithListenAddr, with a test that New with WithWSAddr listens on exactly that address. Fixed by the same commit; the bead exists so the commit can name it and so the missing test is on record.

title: Group defaults reject the auth field the merge actually applies
description:
profile.go:266-277 lists the allowed keys for a group's Defaults, and "auth" is not among them - yet SparseSSHOptions.Auth is a real inheritable field with json tag "auth" (profile.go:244), and the merge applies it (profile.go:588-591). UnmarshalJSON records it as unknown (profile.go:282-300), so Defaults.Validate() (profile.go:338-346) rejects it.

Every write path that calls Validate is affected: CreateGroup (store.go:263), UpdateGroup (store.go:295), ApplyGroups (store.go:405), SaveGroup (service.go:108), AtomicImport (service.go:241).

## Steps to Reproduce

Open a group's editor, set the Auth mode default, save. The write fails with "unknown keys in defaults: auth".

## Acceptance Criteria

"auth" is in allowedFields, with a test that a group carrying an auth default round-trips through create, update and apply. While there, a test that asserts the allow-list and the struct's json tags agree, so the next added field cannot drift the same way.
close_reason: Closed

title: Unvalidated host becomes an ssh -G positional argument
description:
open with kind ssh passes params.Host straight to ResolveConfig (ws.go:759), which builds argv as exec.CommandContext(ctx, sshPath, "-F", configPath, "-G", host) (ssh_resolver.go:232,241). The host is a positional argument with no "--" terminator and no check for a leading dash, and later flags win over earlier ones.

No shell is involved and -G does not connect, so this is argument injection into a fixed binary rather than command execution. It is still an unintended read/write primitive against the ssh client.

## Steps to Reproduce

Call open with host set to a string beginning with a dash that ssh reads as an option - for example one that re-points the config file, overriding the -F the app itself passed.

## Acceptance Criteria

The argv carries "--" before the host, or the host is rejected when it begins with a dash, with a test. Profile Host on profiles.create gets the same treatment: it is equally unchecked and reaches the dialer.

title: rollout.run has no upper bound on concurrency or target count
description:
ws_rollout.go:55-62 checks only that credentialId, versionId and targetIds are non-empty. runner.go:127-132 gives batchSize, globalConcurrency and bastionConcurrency a lower bound only - "if <= 0 { default }" - and nothing bounds them above or bounds len(targetIds). The handler runs on context.Background() (ws_rollout.go:69) with no deadline.

## Steps to Reproduce

Call rollout.run with ten thousand target ids and globalConcurrency 100000. The runner opens outbound SSH handshakes as fast as the OS allows, against the whole fleet, with no deadline and no way to stop it.

## Acceptance Criteria

Upper bounds on batchSize, globalConcurrency and bastionConcurrency, and a cap on len(targetIds), each with a test at the boundary. The run takes a context with a deadline. Note the security framing already recorded for this epic: a burst of authentication attempts across many hosts is indistinguishable from spraying, so the bound is not merely a resource limit.

title: No read limit on the WebSocket: one frame allocates whatever it claims
description:
internal/transport/ws.go:562 calls conn.ReadMessage() on a gorilla Conn whose SetReadLimit is never called - grep finds zero occurrences in the repo, so the limit is unlimited. handleControlFrame (ws.go:576-607) then json.Unmarshals the whole buffer, and DecodeFrame (frame.go:107-121) allocates len(data)-18 with no cap of its own, so a binary frame costs a second copy.

profiles.importTabby (ws.go:1875-1881) is the widest mouth: an arbitrary YAML string parsed whole.

## Steps to Reproduce

Send one text frame of a few hundred megabytes on the control plane. The process buffers all of it before any handler runs.

## Acceptance Criteria

SetReadLimit is called once on the connection with a documented value, and a test asserts a frame above it closes the connection rather than allocating. One limit covers every method, which is why this belongs with the dispatch work rather than with any single handler.

title: NeedsReview is documented as a resolver gate but nothing reads it
description:
profile.go:53-54 says "The resolver refuses profiles with this flag set". It does not: grep across internal/ (tests excluded) finds NeedsReview only in profile.go and service.go, and ErrProfileNeedsReview (service.go:18-24) is returned by nothing. connection/resolver.go never reads the field.

That flag is what AtomicImport sets (service.go:229) for exactly the credential-hijack case in the sibling bug, so the safety net for that import is inert.

## Steps to Reproduce

Import a configuration that trips the AtomicImport review path, so the stored profile carries needsReview. Connect it. The resolver builds a config and dials as though nothing were flagged.

Separately: profiles.update (ws.go:1209-1223) accepts the flag from the renderer, so even once the resolver honours it the renderer can switch it off.

## Acceptance Criteria

The resolver returns ErrProfileNeedsReview for a flagged profile, with a test. The flag is backend-owned on the write path the way credentials.create owns secretId, with a test that a renderer-supplied value is ignored.

title: Promotion, retirement and revocation are three transitions
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

Spec section 6 states these apart deliberately: "Conflating them would drain transports that
are legitimately still running a pinned previous version."

- **promote candidate** — the candidate becomes current. The previous version stays usable for
  profiles explicitly pinned to it, and NOTHING is drained.
- **retire previous** — the version may no longer be selected for new connections; the user
  chooses whether existing transports on it drain (sections 3.7, 3.8).
- **emergency revoke** — a separate destructive action that closes everything using the
  version now.
- Promotion happens on a declared threshold, not on a feeling. State it.
- A straggler pin is keyed by PROFILE PROVENANCE, not by endpoint. Two profiles can share an
  endpoint; pinning one must not pin the other.
- Each transition is testable in isolation, and the test asserts what does NOT happen —
  promotion draining nothing is the property that breaks silently.
close_reason: Three transitions with threshold below the transport, profile-keyed pins, negative tests for promotion draining nothing. Revision pass required for tests and threshold placement.

title: A rollout is a bounded run, not a loop over hosts
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

Spec section 6. Every constraint below is load-bearing; none is optional.

- A canary selection is probed first. The canary is an EPHEMERAL selection, not a persisted
  set — "if it survived across rollouts it would be a fleet under another name, and section 3.3
  chose one tree."
- Rollout proceeds in bounded batches, with per-endpoint status recorded.
- Concurrency is bounded GLOBALLY and PER BASTION, not per target. One dead bastion must be
  reported once, not as forty independent password failures.
- Every probe forces a fresh transport, bypasses the pool, authenticates and closes without
  launching a shell or running a command.
- A probe sends ONLY the intended candidate method — never the full auth chain. MaxAuthTries
  is finite and burning it is how a rollout locks the fleet out.
- NEVER try several passwords against one host. That triggers lockouts and is
  indistinguishable from password spraying.
- Verify the host key BEFORE probing.
- keyboard-interactive and MFA cannot be bulk-probed. Detect and exclude them with a stated
  reason rather than attempting and failing — they need their own interaction model, which is
  not this bead.
- A rollout can be stopped, and stopping leaves a coherent state that says what was reached.

## Note for whoever takes this

The safety constraints above are the reason this epic was held for a session with the owner
present. Build and unit-test it freely; do NOT run it against real hosts without saying so
first.
close_reason: Rollout runner in internal/rollout, wired at app.go, 13 unit + 7 transport tests. Evidence now feeds the promotion threshold (coordinator closed that seam).

title: A probe result knows what it was a result OF, and expires when that changes
description:
## Why this is its own bead

Spec section 6 is exact about it, and a rollout that trusts a stale probe reports a fleet
healthy that is not:

"a probe result is keyed by endpoint, host-key identity, credential version, effective
username and auth policy, plus a timestamp, and is invalidated by any change to the endpoint,
group chain, ~/.ssh/config, host key or credential."

## What exists

connections.test (nocx-uxs5.3, internal/transport/ws_probe.go) probes one target and returns a
typed outcome — accepted, rejected, unreachable, host-key problem, needs-interactive. It has
no notion of a result that persists or expires.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A probe result record carrying the full key above. Not "host + ok"; every component, because
  each one changing makes the answer wrong in a different way.
- Invalidation on any change to those inputs. A group-chain edit that changes the effective
  username invalidates every result computed under the old one — reuse the effective-profile
  engine to notice, do not re-derive.
- Results are operational evidence, not profile configuration (spec section 6). Specify
  retention, manual clearing, and what import/export does with them — the spec asks for this
  explicitly and it is the kind of thing that gets decided by accident.
- Distinguish a network failure from a rejected password. Report "locked" ONLY when the server
  actually says so: generic SSH errors do not carry that, and guessing it is how a UI tells
  someone their account is locked when it is not.
close_reason:
A probe result carries the full section 6 key — endpoint, host-key fingerprint, credential version, effective username, auth policy and timestamp — with invalidation guards and a documented retention/clearing/export policy. connections.test records every classified outcome through it, the store is constructed and injected at the composition root (app.go:98, :114, :190), and TestConnectionsTest_StoresResult fails if that wiring is removed.

The first pass built all of it and wired none of it: nothing constructed the store and nothing called ProbeConfigWithResult. That was reported honestly, which is why it was a revision rather than a rewrite, but it would have been the fourth instance this session of code unreachable from main() — and the first one this session would have INTRODUCED rather than inherited. The blocker named (host-key fingerprint unavailable through Prober) was solved by widening the narrow transport-declared interface, the pattern app.go already uses twice.

title: A credential can stage a candidate version without disturbing the current one
description:
## What exists

Wave 1 shipped the model: Credential.Versions, CurrentVersionID, CandidateVersionID
(internal/profile/credential.go). CandidateVersionID is documented there as "Unused until wave
8 — carried here so the model exists, not built on". This is wave 8.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A candidate version can be created with its own secret material, without touching the
  current one. Creating it changes nothing about how ordinary connections authenticate.
- The secret goes through the same backend-owned path as any other; the renderer never sees or
  transmits a secret reference (ADR-0011).
- Staging is reversible: a candidate can be discarded before any rollout begins.
- Only one candidate at a time, or state deliberately what several would mean.
- An ordinary connection uses CURRENT. Never candidate, never a fallback between them. Spec
  section 6: "Forbidden: a candidate rejection followed by an invisible retry with the current
  version during an ordinary connection — it hides rollout state and spends extra
  authentication attempts." Test that an ordinary connect with a candidate staged still
  authenticates with current, and that a failure does not silently try the other one.

## Deliberately out

Rollout orchestration, probing, promotion. Those are siblings. This bead is the staging
ground they stand on.
close_reason:
credentials.stagePassword creates a candidate with its own secret and leaves CurrentVersionID untouched; credentials.discardCandidate removes it and its secret, idempotently; one candidate at a time is enforced at the store layer. Secrets go through the existing backend-owned path — the renderer never sees a reference.

The no-silent-fallback invariant holds, and by construction rather than by guard: the resolver publishes exactly one secret reference, from cred.Current() (resolver.go:159-165), and internal/ssh has no knowledge of Versions or Candidate at all, so the dial path cannot reach a second version. TestResolve_UsesCurrentVersionSecret pins it with a credential carrying TWO versions, asserts only current's secret crosses, and asserts the SecretID CHANGES on promotion — because an unchanged one would let the pool reuse the old transport (spec 3.7).

Coordinator note: the brief demanded a separate test that a failed connect does not retry with the other version. That was a wrong instruction — no such mechanism exists to assert the absence of, so the test would have passed trivially and kept passing if the mechanism were later added elsewhere. nocx-383c.3 is where internal/ssh first gains version knowledge, deliberately, and its brief must carry the constraint.

title: Changed lines must be covered, or the gate says so
description:
## Why this ranks above mutation testing

Measured against the 2026-07-29 session, where thirteen defects were found by reading diffs
rather than by any gate:

- Nine were tests that did NOT EXIST. Two of those were large: a 653-line rewrite of the
  connection list with zero tests, and the group editor with zero tests. Both were caught only
  because the coordinator counted `it(` blocks before and after, and both reports quoted a
  passing suite total another wave had produced — true, and misleading.
- One would have been caught by mutation testing (a nil slice where the wire contract required
  an empty array; the assertion `len() == 0` could not tell them apart).
- Three were reachability, which neither tool looks at (nocx-nc4i).

A changed-line coverage gate catches the nine directly and cheaply. Mutation testing (nocx-u4b,
nocx-ckoy.5) is the refinement that comes AFTER coverage exists — it measures whether existing
assertions are strong, which is a question you can only ask once there are assertions.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A gate reports coverage for the lines a commit or PR changes, for both Go and TypeScript,
  and fails on new uncovered lines rather than on a whole-repo percentage. A repo-wide number
  moves too slowly to notice a single untested feature landing.
- It runs where it does not cost the commit: the pre-commit hook was brought from 67s to 3-29s
  deliberately (nocx-ro3h) and must not regress. CI on a PR is the natural home; note that CI
  currently runs only on PRs to main and release branches.
- Existing uncovered code is baselined per item, the way ADR-0014 baselines raw-control
  violations: stale entries harmless, growth an error. A global percentage threshold is not
  acceptable — it is the form that gets gamed.
- The failure names the file and lines, so the fix is obvious rather than a hunt.

## The trap to write into the config

Coverage measures execution, not assertion. A test that calls a function and asserts nothing
raises the number. This gate exists to catch ABSENCE, not to certify quality — say so where
the threshold is configured, so the next person does not mistake a green gate for a tested
feature.

title: ssh -G replaces the library as the ssh_config resolver
description:
## What changes

internal/ssh/ssh_config.go resolves aliases through github.com/kevinburke/ssh_config. That
library does not support Match, and a Match block anywhere in the file makes Decode fail, at
which point ResolveHostName silently returns the original host — every alias in the file stops
resolving and nobody is told (nocx-n7yv).

Replace it: ask `ssh -G <host>` and parse its answer. The reference implementation is the
oracle.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A resolver behind an interface, injected at the composition root — not a package-level
  function reaching for os/exec wherever it is called.
- Results are cached. The motivating case is forty hosts; forty subprocesses on one list
  render is not the design. State the invalidation rule deliberately: mtime of the config
  files, a TTL, or explicit refresh — and say why in a comment.
- **Honest degradation, stated in one place**: no ssh binary, ssh -G failing, or ssh -G being
  slow are three different conditions and must not all collapse into "no config". The user is
  told, once, not on every connect.
- The existing callers — ResolveHostName and resolveAuthzEndpoint — go through it. Note that
