title: Probe reports no-service when the Secret Service is running but its collection is unusable
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Found by accident while verifying nocx-25k9.2 with a deliberately incomplete recipe:

    nix-shell -p gnome-keyring dbus --run 'dbus-run-session -- bash -c "echo -n test | gnome-keyring-daemon --unlock; go test ./internal/vault/system/ -run TestRealKeyring -v"'

That starts the daemon and registers org.freedesktop.secrets but never creates a usable login collection. Result:

- SecretServiceAvailable() returns TRUE — the D-Bus name has an owner — so the integration test runs instead of skipping.
- Probe() then fails its write and reports Ready=false, Reason="no-service".

Both halves are wrong in a way that matters.

## Why it matters

The reason codes exist so the UI can offer the right remedy. 'no-service' tells the user to install and start a keyring they demonstrably already have running; the truthful answers are 'locked' or 'denied'. This is precisely the misdiagnosis the machine-readable discriminator was introduced to prevent, so it is worth fixing even though it is not release-blocking.

Secondly, the guard and the probe disagree about what available means. The test skips on SecretServiceAvailable and asserts on Probe, so a half-working store produces a FAILING test rather than a skipped one — noise that looks like a real regression.

## Note for whoever picks this up

The full CI recipe (gnome-keyring-daemon --daemonize --login, then --unlock) works and the integration test passes all seven subtests against it. This bug is only about the partial state, which is a realistic thing to hit on a user machine — a running daemon with a locked or missing collection.
acceptance_criteria: With a Secret Service whose bus name is owned but whose collection cannot be written, Probe reports a reason distinguishable from 'no service at all' — locked or denied, not no-service. SecretServiceAvailable and Probe agree on what 'available' means, or the integration test guards on the one it asserts against, so a half-working store makes the test skip rather than fail.
notes:
Reproduced against a real locked collection on 2026-07-30, and the reproduction is not reliable — both facts matter.

Recipe (probe = a tiny main calling system.New().Probe):
  nix-shell -p gnome-keyring dbus --run 'dbus-run-session -- bash -c "
    eval $(echo -n nocx-ci | gnome-keyring-daemon --daemonize --login)
    echo -n nocx-ci | gnome-keyring-daemon --unlock
    <probe>                # READY=true REASON=""
    dbus-send --session --dest=org.freedesktop.secrets --print-reply --type=method_call \
      /org/freedesktop/secrets org.freedesktop.Secret.Service.Lock \
      array:objpath:/org/freedesktop/secrets/collection/login
    <probe>                # READY=false REASON="no-service"   <-- the defect
  "'

So a locked collection is reported as 'no system keyring available' and the user is told to invent a master passphrase instead of being told to unlock their login keychain.

On a second attempt the same recipe gave READY=true after the Lock: a daemon started with --login holds the password and re-unlocks on the next access. Any test built on this needs a daemon that cannot self-unlock, or the arrangement will pass by accident.

Note also that classifyReason (internal/vault/system/system.go:282) guesses from error text — strings.Contains(s, "locked"). The raw error for the locked case was never captured, because the run that reproduced the defect did not print it and the run that printed it did not reproduce. Fixing the classifier against a string nobody has seen would be guesswork; the robust alternative is to read the collection's Locked property over D-Bus rather than infer it, which is a real dependency decision and should be made deliberately.
close_reason: Reason is now observed over D-Bus rather than guessed from go-keyring's error text. Verified against a real gnome-keyring: locking the login collection turns READY=false REASON="no-service" into REASON="locked", and SecretServiceAvailable now means usable so the integration test skips instead of failing. Confirmed the stricter guard does NOT make Linux CI skip: under the full CI recipe AVAILABLE=true and both TestRealKeyring tests run and pass.

title: Two app instances would silently lose each other's writes, and not only in the vault
description:
Raised by the vault core review but NOT vault-specific, so it is filed outside that epic.

Every DocumentStore consumer loads its document once into memory and later writes the whole thing back atomically. Atomic rename prevents a torn file; it does not prevent last-writer-wins loss between two processes. profiles.json has had this property since it was written — the vault simply makes the consequence sharper, because losing a journal entry or a key envelope is not the same as losing a profile edit.

A second app instance is not exotic: a user double-launches, or a stale process survives a crash. Wails runs one backend per process, so two instances are two writers.

Options, in rough order of cost: document the invariant and add a startup check that detects an existing instance and refuses or hands off; or take an inter-process lock over the config directory for the lifetime of the process; or accept it explicitly and say so in the ADR. What is not acceptable is the current state, where the behaviour is undefined and undocumented.
acceptance_criteria: Either the single-backend-process invariant is documented and enforced with a startup check that refuses or defers to an existing instance, or an inter-process lock guards the config directory. Whichever is chosen is written down and covered by a test.

title: V1.14 A real Secret Service in Linux CI, so the system provider is actually tested
description:

Spec: .internal/specs/2026-07-30-vault-storage-backend-design.md

## Acceptance Criteria

The Linux job installs gnome-keyring and dbus-x11 and runs the Go suite under dbus-run-session with an unlocked collection. An integration test runs against the REAL go-keyring in that job and skips elsewhere with a clear message. The job proves both paths: one run with the Secret Service present, one without. An integration test runs against the REAL go-keyring in that job and skips elsewhere with a clear message. The job proves both paths: one run with the Secret Service present, one without. Reading the CI log to confirm the keyring test RAN rather than skipped is not possible before a push — filed separately.

title: Step 7: spec self-review (placeholders, consistency, scope, ambiguity)
close_reason: Self-review found five under-specified points, all fixed inline: how the ctx-free SecretStore supplies a ctx to providers; that passphrase/recovery envelopes exist only once created; what unseal actually looks like on a keychain machine (one click, no prompt); that the sealed visibility rule is realised in V2 while V1 ships only the backend refusal; and that a locked system store reports 'unavailable' rather than earning an untestable third Status value. No placeholders, no contradictions found.

title: Step 9: optional stress-test if selected at the spec gate
close_reason: The stress-test step was served by an adversarial peer review against codex (thread 019fb218) rather than the stress-test skill, at the owner's instruction. It overturned four positions: the vault catalogue (second metadata owner, and a second document breaks AtomicImport), the dropped journal (ADR-0011 §4 requires one), Set vs a Vault-owned Create, and two overclaimed guarantees (ctx cannot cancel a go-keyring call; seal cannot revoke an already-issued Secret). It also surfaced the open Reveal-vs-ADR-0011-§2 question. Spec revised and committed at 79f06a6.

title: Names and minted ids have no length cap
description:
slugify (profile.go:775-789) is allow-list-by-construction - it lowercases and keeps [a-z0-9_-], replacing everything else with a dash - so "../../etc" becomes "-----etc" and traversal through an id is not reachable. Confirmed separately that no renderer string reaches any filepath.Join in internal/: documentStore joins only its own fixed name (storage/document.go:111) and profiles, groups and credentials all live in one JSON document (store.go:93-97).

What is missing is a length cap. A 10 MB name yields a 10 MB id through NewProfileID (profile.go:745), NewGroupID (profile.go:755) and NewCredentialID (credential.go:194). No Name field has a length or charset check anywhere, and the ids are stored, exported, and echoed back.

Filed as a task rather than a bug: nothing is exploitable today, the store is the only consumer, and the fix belongs with whatever nocx-98rn establishes.

## Acceptance Criteria

Name and id length are capped at the point they are minted and at the point they are accepted, with a test at the boundary. The cap is one constant, not one per call site.

title: Three smaller unvalidated inputs: keyPath, empty host, unowned ack
description:
Three smaller holes found in the same audit, grouped because each is a couple of lines and they share a fix shape.

1. keyPath reaches os.ReadFile with no restriction. credentials.create/update accept it verbatim (ws.go:1383, ws.go:1481); it flows cred.KeyPath -> cfg.KeyFile (connection/resolver.go:185) -> resolved.identityFile (ssh_config.go:76-78) -> os.ReadFile (ssh_auth.go:193), with only ~/ expanded. connections.test then reports the outcome, which makes it a file-existence and parse oracle over the filesystem.

2. profiles.create stores a profile with an empty host. ws.go:1194-1223 goes from json.Unmarshal to JSONStore.CreateProfile, which checks only that the id is non-empty (store.go:164-167). ProfileService.SaveProfile:70 does require a host and is not reachable from this method.

3. ack does not check the session belongs to the connection (ws.go:1003-1021), unlike resize and close which do.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Save a credential with keyPath /etc/shadow and run connections.test; the error text distinguishes "cannot read" from "not a key".
2. Call profiles.create with no host; the profile is stored and appears in the list.
3. Call ack with another connection's sessionId.

## Acceptance Criteria

Each of the three has a test that fails without its fix. keyPath is either constrained to a base directory or the failure text stops distinguishing cases; profiles.create requires a host on the same path SaveProfile does; ack checks connection ownership the way resize does.

title: The rollout has a surface that shows what is true
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- Staging a candidate, choosing a canary, watching a rollout, and the three transitions are
  reachable from the Credentials section.
- Per-endpoint status distinguishes accepted, rejected, unreachable, host-key problem and
  needs-interactive — the taxonomy the probe already returns. Do not invent a second one.
- The blast radius of a transition is shown before it is applied, the way group changes do
  (nocx-uxs5.11). Emergency revoke closes live transports; that must not be a single
  unqualified button.
- Rollout status is operational evidence, not profile configuration. It reads as a run that
  happened, not as settings.
- Accessibility is acceptance criteria: destructive confirmations announced, focus restored.

## Deliberately out

Anything that starts a real rollout without the user asking for it.
close_reason: Rollout surface in credentials section: staging, canary, run, per-endpoint taxonomy with exclusions and not-attempted apart, impact preview before every destructive transition. Coordinator repaired a broken Dialog tag and an invalid role=list.

title: Save as connection adopts an external host
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

Spec section 4.

- After connecting to an alias that came from ~/.ssh/config, the user can save it as a nocx
  connection.
- The saved profile stores the ALIAS, not the resolved hostname — the point is to keep
  following the live source, not to freeze one evaluation of it.
- Once saved, the system duplicate is suppressed (the rule from the palette bead).
close_reason: Save as connection stores the ALIAS, not the resolved hostname, so the adopted profile keeps following the live config and the palette's suppression — which compares alias to profile host — removes the system entry for free. user and port are carried only when the config supplied them. Coordinator fixed three things at integration: the renderer minted a profile id again (nocx-uxs5.10 removed that; the backend mints on profiles.create), the caller discarded the returned record and logged an empty id, and a restored test asserted the old minting behaviour. The report also claimed to have fixed a broken alias session path; the branch shows the path was sound and the actual change was port plumbing.

title: A terminal hint offers the alias the user is typing
description:
## Scope, and its honest limit

Spec section 4. The hint is FRONTEND-only. AD-6 forbids the backend interpreting the byte
stream, so it cannot be built there.

nocx knows the command text only while its own command editor owns input — submission runs
through ShellInputTarget (terminal-content.ts). In raw terminal mode it does not: OSC 133
marks prompt and command boundaries but does not expose the shell current editable line, and
reconstructing `ssh <host>` from keystrokes is unreliable because history, completion, cursor
movement and pasted control sequences are handled remotely.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Typing `ssh <partial>` in the nocx command editor offers matching aliases.
- Raw terminal mode is NOT promised. Do not attempt it; supporting arbitrary native shell
  input needs cooperating shell integration (AD-5 Tier B) and is a separate decision.
- The limit is visible to the user rather than felt as flakiness.
close_reason: Typing ssh <partial> in the nocx command editor offers matching aliases, fetched live per keystroke generation with stale-response gating — no cached snapshot, so the hint cannot go stale behind the palette. Raw mode degrades transparently. Coordinator rewired it onto the shared contract: the worker built its own SSHConfigAlias types and listSSHConfigAliases method in profiles.ts despite the brief giving that ownership to the palette worker, so there were briefly two client methods for one RPC. Its private wildcard filter was deleted rather than renamed — the backend already excludes patterns in containsWildcard, and the two copies had already drifted, the frontend regex covering brackets and braces while missing '!'. 994 tests.

title: Aliases from ~/.ssh/config are a live source in the quick-connect palette
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

Spec section 4.

- Aliases appear in the quick-connect palette as a LIVE, read-only source — never copied.
- They do NOT appear in the connection manager, which lists only nocx-owned records, so an
  empty manager honestly means "you have not saved any connections".
- **Priority is ours**: when a saved profile targets the same alias, the system duplicate is
  not offered. Alias identity must be defined precisely and in one place — a profile named
  differently but pointing at the same alias is the same target and must also suppress the
  duplicate. Write that rule down where it is enforced, not in two places.
- The source is visibly distinguishable from a saved connection, so the user knows which one
  nocx owns.
close_reason: sshConfig.aliases enumerates Host patterns from ~/.ssh/config and resolves each one's values through the ssh -G resolver — enumeration and authority are deliberately separate, and the narrow scan says so in its own comment so nobody mistakes it for a second parser. Wildcards are excluded on the backend, in one place. A saved profile whose host equals the alias suppresses the system entry, and the profile's NAME plays no part, so a differently-named profile targeting the same alias suppresses it too. An unreadable config surfaces through the unavailable field rather than looking like an empty list — the failure nocx-n7yv was. Coordinator fixed three lint findings the worker reported as clean: an unchecked defer Close, an unjustified G304, and 0644 fixture permissions on an ssh config.

title: Creation starts from one field
description:
## Acceptance Criteria

- Creating a connection starts from a single field accepting deploy@10.0.0.1:2222, a bare
  alias, or ssh://...
- parseQuickConnect (frontend/src/profiles.ts) already does this parsing and is currently
  reached only from the palette. Reuse it; do not write a second parser.
- What could not be parsed is stated, not silently dropped.
close_reason: Creating a connection starts from one field accepting deploy@10.0.0.1:2222, a bare alias or ssh://. parseQuickConnect was EXTENDED for the ssh:// scheme rather than duplicated — the constraint that mattered, given three earlier revisions in this epic were sent back for a second implementation that had to agree with a first. Unparseable input is stated, not dropped.

title: TextField composes Field, so the kit stops carrying two label implementations
description:
## What is wrong

frontend/src/ui/text-field.tsx implements its own label, and frontend/src/ui/field.tsx
implements another. Spec section 5 names the consequence: the required marker exists in one
of them, so it appears on some controls and not others depending on which the surface reached
for. Two vocabularies for one concept is the defect the kit migration spent two epics
unwinding.

## Acceptance Criteria

- TextField composes Field rather than duplicating it. The required marker, label, error and
  description come from one implementation.
- Every existing caller keeps working with no change at its call site, or the change is
  mechanical and applied here.
- The kit README inventory table reflects the composition.
- Identity classes stay stable: the CSS-integrity and kit-identity lint gates must still pass,
  and the raw-controls / inline-markup baselines must not grow. If a baseline entry becomes
  stale that is fine; growth is not.
- Existing kit tests still pass and the composition is covered.

## Why this is its own bead

It is the one piece of wave 6 that touches only frontend/src/ui/, so it runs in parallel with
the backend without colliding with the surface rewrite that follows.
close_reason: TextField composes Field; one label implementation, so the required marker is everywhere at once. Coordinator fixed an accessibility regression the composition introduced — label={props.label!} silenced a real case and emitted an empty <label for> for a field with only an error. Field.label is now optional and the element is omitted when empty; both directions pinned by tests. Commit d01ca47.

title: Wiring global defaults must extend the credential-usage contract
description:
## What this is

`ComputeCredentialUsage` (internal/profile/usage.go) reports where a profile got its
credential: `source: "profile" | "group"`. Those are the only two values the renderer
switches on, and they are the only two the effective-profile engine can produce today.

`FieldSourceGlobal` (internal/profile/profile.go:245) is documented as "not yet wired to a
store", and the transport passes an empty `SparseSSHOptions{}`. `FieldSourceDefault` cannot
supply a credentialId — the hardcoded defaults are port, user and behaviorOnSessionEnd.

So a profile whose credential comes from a global default is impossible now, and the
computation skips that case rather than emitting an undocumented third source value into the
wire contract.

## Why this is a bead and not a comment

The day global defaults get a store, that skip becomes silent undercounting: a credential
used by every profile through a global default would report "not used by anything", and the
delete confirmation would show an empty blast radius for a credential the whole fleet uses.
Nothing would fail; the number would just be wrong.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Whoever wires global defaults to a store extends the usage contract with the third source
  and ships the renderer's handling of it in the same wave.
- The skip in usage.go is replaced, not merely widened, and a test covers a profile whose
  credential arrives from a global default.
- The contract change is reflected wherever it is written down (the wave-5 briefs and any
  ADR that carries it).
notes: Resolved in part during wave 5: the third source value 'global' now exists in the contract (ProfileRefSourceGlobal, internal/profile/usage.go) rather than being silently dropped. What remains is what the title says — wiring global defaults to a store, and the renderer's handling of the third value. The coordinator's first attempt was to skip the case entirely; the backend worker's TestComputeCredentialUsage_GlobalDefaultsInherited caught it, which is why the skip is not what shipped.

title: ADR-0006 describes the credential model that shipped
description:
## What is wrong today

`docs/decisions/0006-reusable-credentials.md` documents a model the code stopped having,
and it has been contradicting itself since wave 2 landed:

- Line 27 still carries `Host string // Optional: bind to specific host (empty = works for
  any host)`. `nocx-mon` made an empty host a refusal at connect time, and wave 2
  (`nocx-j685`) then deleted the field outright. Go's `Credential`
  (`internal/profile/credential.go:20`) has no `Host` at all.
- The "UI Changes" section describes a "Saved Credentials (УЗ) button" that opens a form.
  Wave 5 deletes that button — an entity switch disguised as an action — in favour of a
  Credentials entry in the settings rail.
- The storage section predates credential versions (wave 1): `Versions`,
  `CurrentVersionID`, `CandidateVersionID` do not appear in the ADR at all.

An ADR that describes a model nobody implements is worse than no ADR: it is the document
the next agent will believe.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The Data Model block matches `internal/profile/credential.go` as shipped, including the
  version fields and what each is for.
- Authorization is described as computed from the profiles that reference the credential
  (spec section 3.1). The host binding is recorded as **removed**, with the reason and the
  work that removed it — do not silently delete the paragraph. An ADR that quietly loses a
  decision destroys the only record of why the decision was made.
- The UI section describes the Credentials settings section and the one shared form
  component that both it and the wave-6 dialog host.
- The amendment is dated and attributed the way ADR-0001 records its 2026-07-26 amendment;
  the header's Status/Date reflect it.

## Deliberately out

The vault-versus-keychain question (`nocx-25k9`). Where secrets physically live is not what
this ADR decides, and guessing at it here would create a second contradiction to unwind.
close_reason: ADR-0006 now describes the shipped model: versions, no host binding, computed authorization, CredentialPatch, and the settings-rail section. The removed host-binding rule is recorded with its reasoning rather than deleted.

title: Changing a fleet password is a rollout, not a hope
description: Wave 8. Spec sections 3.9 and 6. SAFETY: never try several passwords against one host — it triggers account lockouts and is indistinguishable from password spraying. MaxAuthTries is finite. Verify the host key before probing. Built on the probe primitive from wave 4 and the version model from wave 1.
acceptance_criteria: A credential holds current and candidate versions; a canary selection is probed with a forced-fresh pool-bypassing connection sending only the intended method; per-endpoint status distinguishes accepted, rejected, unreachable, host-key problem and needs-interactive; rollout proceeds in bounded batches with per-bastion concurrency limits; promotion, retirement and emergency revocation are three distinct transitions; there is never a silent fallback from candidate to current during an ordinary connection; a straggler pin is keyed by profile provenance, not by endpoint.
close_reason: All five children closed. Criterion met clause by clause: versions model (8.1); canary probed first through a forced-fresh pool-bypassing single-method probe (8.3 + ssh_probe.go); five-outcome taxonomy in ssh.ClassifyProbeError and rendered as such (8.5); bounded batches with global and per-bastion concurrency (8.3); three distinct transitions (8.4); no silent candidate-to-current fallback (ResolveWithVersion, tested); pin keyed by profile provenance, tested that pinning one profile does not pin another on a shared endpoint. NOT run against real hosts — that needs the owner present.

title: Hosts from ~/.ssh/config appear where they are looked for
description: Wave 7. Spec section 4. The terminal hint is frontend-only and works while nocx's command editor owns input — OSC 133 marks command boundaries but does not expose the shell's editable line, so raw-shell support needs cooperating shell integration and is NOT promised here. AD-6 forbids building any of it on the backend.
acceptance_criteria: ~/.ssh/config aliases are a live read-only source surfaced in the quick-connect palette and in a terminal hint inside the nocx command editor; the connection manager still lists only nocx-owned records; a saved profile targeting the same alias suppresses the system duplicate; Save as connection adopts an external host storing the alias; a one-off importer exists alongside the Tabby one, labelled as producing a detached copy; the supported ssh_config subset is declared and conformance-tested against ssh -G.
close_reason: Wave 7 landed in five commits (6ce3063, f519d28, 234fbfd, 01a4463, f4a1bd2). nocx stopped parsing ~/.ssh/config and asks ssh -G instead (ADR-0015), which closed nocx-n7yv — a single Match directive had silently disabled every alias. Aliases are a live read-only source in the palette and in the command editor's hint, suppressed when a saved profile targets the same alias; Save as connection adopts one by storing the alias, and a separate importer produces an honestly-labelled detached copy storing the resolved hostname. The supported-subset and conformance-fixture task from spec section 9 item 3 dissolved: the subset is whatever the user's ssh supports, and make conformance checks the parsing against the real binary.

title: e2e/proof-matrix.spec.ts: unused initialId fails npx eslint . on the branch
description:
\`npx eslint .\` at the repo root reports one error on the branch, introduced by
bbd8723 and unrelated to any work in flight: e2e/proof-matrix.spec.ts:573 assigns
\`initialId\` from the active tab's data-tab-id and never reads it. The assertion
that followed it was replaced by one that reads the first tab directly, and the
binding was left behind.

It matters because AGENTS.md makes \`npx eslint .\` part of the gate that runs
before every push, so a single dead binding blocks every unrelated change until
someone removes it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. \`npx eslint .\` from the repo root.
2. One error: '@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars' at e2e/proof-matrix.spec.ts:573.

## Acceptance Criteria

- \`npx eslint .\` exits clean at the repo root.
- The ArrowLeft focus-movement assertion in that test still checks what it checked.
close_reason: Deleted the unused initialId binding in e2e/proof-matrix.spec.ts; npx eslint . is clean at the repo root. Commit 2245418.

title: e2e activity-bell waits on the app alt-screen class that nocx-6w4z deleted
description:
nocx-6w4z moved the fullscreen live region inside the pane and deleted the
`#app.alt-screen` class it replaced (the class existed to blank the window
chrome that the old viewport-sized xterm painted over). e2e/activity-bell still
waited on that class, so it timed out 5s into a spec whose actual subject — a
bell lighting the tab indicator from the alternate buffer — was never reached.

Retargeted at `.pane.active .xterm-live-container.live-fullscreen`, which is
what `enterFullscreen()` writes on the same alt-screen path.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run e2e/activity-bell.spec.ts on main at 6efb1bf: it fails with
`toHaveClass(/alt-screen/) ... Received: ""`.

## Acceptance Criteria

e2e/activity-bell passes in chromium and webkit, and asserts alt-screen through
a class the product still sets.
close_reason: Spec retargeted at .xterm-live-container.live-fullscreen

title: DocumentStore path capability does not confine names to its root
description:
DocumentStore.pathFor blindly filepath.Join values supplied by callers. Absolute paths and parent traversal can escape the configured root, and the symlink check is separated from rename by a TOCTOU window. Current production callers pass constants, but the capability boundary is weaker than ADR-0011 states and becomes unsafe for future plugins or importers.

## Steps to Reproduce

Construct a DocumentStore rooted in a temporary directory and call Write with an absolute name or a parent traversal name. The resolved target can leave the configured root; a concurrent symlink replacement can also race the pre-rename check.
acceptance_criteria: Document names are validated as root-relative basenames or an explicitly documented safe relative form; absolute paths, traversal and symlink escapes are rejected. Tests prove writes cannot leave the configured root under hostile names and symlink replacement.

title: Session output pump can busy-loop on a zero-length successful read
description:
realSession.readPump immediately calls the output handler after Read returns n=0, err=nil and repeats without blocking or yielding. A legal but misbehaving Channel implementation can consume a CPU core and flood the handler with empty slices.

## Steps to Reproduce

Use a Channel fake whose Read repeatedly returns zero, nil. Start output and observe the loop repeatedly invoke the handler without waiting.
acceptance_criteria: A zero-length successful read cannot spin or invoke the output handler repeatedly; the policy is documented and tested with a channel that returns consecutive zero-length reads before data or EOF.

title: Замороженный блок переносит строки не так, как терминал: метрики шрифта блока не совпадают с сеткой xterm
description:
## Проблема

Замороженный блок — HTML с white-space: pre-wrap (.cmd-output, style.css:424); браузер переносит его по своим метрикам шрифта, тогда как xterm рисует фиксированную сетку. serializeRange вдобавок намеренно склеивает soft-wrap ("REFLOW (owner directive)"). В результате строка, занимавшая ровно ширину сетки, в блоке не помещается: полноширинная линейка ──── разваливается на длинную строку плюс обрубок, а абзац переносится в других местах, чем видел пользователь.

Арифметика со скриншотов пользователя (2026-07-28): линейка claude = 152 символа, в блок влезает 140 → обрубок ровно на 12 символов, что и видно вторым отрезком. Расхождение метрик ≈ 8.6%.

Замер в .cmd-output (headless Chromium): X = 9.59px, i = 3.89px, ─ = 8.43px — шрифт блока вообще НЕ моноширинный. Стек `ui-monospace, "SF Mono", Menlo, Monaco, ...` (renderers/font.ts и --font-family-mono) на Linux не содержит ни одного существующего семейства, и fontconfig подставляет пропорциональное. На WebKitGTK не мерено — проверить отдельно.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Запустить команду, печатающую строку во всю ширину терминала: `printf "%0.s─" $(seq 1 $(tput cols)); echo`
2. Дождаться завершения. В живой области линия ровно во всю ширину; в блоке она переносится и оставляет короткий хвост на следующей строке.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Строка шириной ровно в сетку PTY занимает в замороженном блоке ровно одну визуальную строку.
- Колоночный вывод (таблицы, ls, псевдографика) в блоке выровнен так же, как в живой области — то есть блок рендерится действительно моноширинным шрифтом с той же продвижкой, что использует сетка xterm.
- Решено явно, что делать с reflow при resize окна (сохранить намеренную перекладку или отказаться в пользу точной сетки) — иначе эти две цели противоречат друг другу.

title: Validation: move focus to the first invalid field and announce the count on submit
description:
`ui/validation.ts` covers the rules and the show-it-yet decision, and the Connections
form refuses an invalid submit with a per-field message plus a toast carrying the first
one. Two things nocx-74cn's design section asked for are not built:

- On a refused submit, focus does not move to the first invalid control. On a form as
  long as the profile editor the offending field can be scrolled out of view; the toast
  names it but the caret stays where it was.
- Nothing announces how many fields failed. A screen-reader user gets the first message
  through the toast region and no count.

## Acceptance Criteria

A refused submit focuses the first failing control and the live region states how many
fields need attention.

title: Export page: manifest, backup payload and status all had surface-only styling
description:
Follow-up found while fixing nocx-kjjs. The export surface owned the appearance of
three things the kit should own, each with its own type size, colours and spacing:

- the mode manifest (`.st-export-manifest` + five sibling classes) — the page's main
  reading matter, sitting two type steps below the text around it;
- the backup payload `<pre>` (`.st-export-backup-details`) — background, border,
  radius, padding, size and scroll cap declared on the surface;
- the outcome line (`.st-export-status`) — see nocx-4clc.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings → Export / Backup / Import.
2. Compare the manifest text size against the summary line above it.
3. Show Backup Paths and look at the payload block.

## Acceptance Criteria

`MarkerList` and `CodeBlock` exist in `ui/`, the export surface imports them, and
`export.css` holds only placement plus the page's own two text styles.

title: Export page: native file-picker button, tiny manifest text, stretched buttons
description:
Three visual defects on Export / Backup / Import:

- `FileInput` renders a bare `input[type=file]`, so the platform draws its own button
  ("Выбор файла" on a Russian browser) inside an English form. ADR-0014 accepted this
  trade; it reads as pasted-in and the kit now wraps the input instead.
- The manifest list (`.st-export-manifest li`, incl. `.st-export-carries`) is at
  `--font-size-xs` — smaller than the summary above it for the page's main content.
- Buttons inside a `Stack` stretch to full width, so Import and Decrypt and Import
  are page-wide slabs while Export Configuration (not in a Stack) is button-sized.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings → Export / Backup / Import.
2. Compare the Configuration Export section with the Import section at the bottom.

## Acceptance Criteria

FileInput shows a kit Button plus the chosen file name; the manifest reads at the same
size as the rest of the page; action buttons size to their label everywhere.

title: Settings: heading floats too far above the first row
description:
The section h2 in the settings surface carried `margin-bottom: var(--space-2)` on top of
PageSection's flex gap (`--space-4`), and `.ui-settings-row` adds its own `--space-3` top
padding: 8 + 16 + 12 = 36px between the heading rule and the first control it names.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the Settings surface, pick any section (e.g. Clipboard).
2. Measure from the h2's bottom border to the first row's label.

## Acceptance Criteria

The heading rule sits one gap above the first row: h2 margin 0, and the flex gap on
`.ui-settings .ui-page-section` alone owns the distance (`--space-2`).

title: Switching strip orientation marks every inactive tab as having activity
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open four tabs and let them sit idle at a prompt.
2. Switch the tab strip from vertical to horizontal.

Expected: nothing changes about the tabs. Changing how the strip is drawn is not
something that happens IN a tab.
Actual: every inactive tab lights its activity indicator.

## Cause

Not a state-storage bug in the strip — the flag really is being set. Switching
orientation resizes every pane at once, `renderer.onResize` sends the new
geometry to the PTY, and the shell answers by redrawing its prompt. That redraw
arrives on `session.onData`, where `terminal-content.ts` calls
`host.requestAttention()` for any output in the normal buffer.

So the output is real; what is wrong is the meaning attached to it. The activity
flag means "output arrived that you have not seen", and output the app provoked
by resizing the window is not that.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Switching orientation leaves every tab activity flag as it was.
- Resizing the window by dragging does the same.
- Output that genuinely arrives on an inactive tab still raises the indicator —
  the suppression is bounded to the shell response to a resize we sent, not a
  general mute.
close_reason: Output that follows a resize we sent is no longer read as unread activity. Switching orientation resizes every pane, the shell redraws its prompt, and that redraw arrived on session.onData looking exactly like output nobody had seen.

title: Active and inactive rows in the vertical strip differ by two percent
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Switch the tab strip to vertical.
2. Open three tabs and look at which one is selected.

Expected: the current tab is obvious.
Actual: the rows read as one undifferentiated column. The only thing separating
them is the 2px indicator on the left edge.

## Measured

Inactive row: `--color-surface-sunken` = #24283b.
Selected row: `--color-tab-active` = #1f2235.

Five, six and six steps out of 255 apart — and in the darker direction.

## Why darker-when-active is wrong here

That is the horizontal strip metaphor: the selected tab drops out of the strip
and merges into the terminal below it, and the shared edge is what sells it. A
vertical row has no edge to share, because the pane is beside the strip rather
than under it. So the metaphor buys nothing and spends the only cue available on
it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The selected row is distinguishable from an inactive one without looking for
  the indicator.
- The device is one the app already uses, not a new value chosen here.
- Applies to the vertical placement only; the horizontal strip keeps the
  merge-with-content treatment, which works because it has the edge for it.
close_reason: Accent tint mixed with the row's own fill, not with transparency. Measured, the two rows differed by five, six and six steps out of 255 and in the darker direction; the first fix made it darker still, because a translucent fill composites over the strip behind it at #0e0f15.

title: The vertical strip's activity indicator is a horizontal underline
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Switch the tab strip to vertical.
2. Make an inactive tab produce output.

Expected: a mark on that row, in the same visual language as the rest of the
vertical strip.
Actual: a 2px underline along the row bottom edge, inset 10px from each side —
the horizontal strip geometry unchanged. A row in a vertical strip has no
meaningful bottom edge, because the next row starts there, so it reads as a
divider between two tabs rather than as a mark on one of them.

## Second half: it shares the accent with the selection bar

Both were `--color-accent`. In the horizontal strip the two were told apart by
which edge they sat on, top versus bottom. That distinction does not survive the
vertical strip, where the selection indicator is a left-edge bar and the activity
mark should be one too.

## Acceptance Criteria

- In vertical placement the activity mark is a left-edge bar, not an underline.
- It is inset from top and bottom where the selection bar runs the full height,
  so the two differ in shape as well as colour.
- Its colour is the warning token, not the accent.
- It is not dimmed. The one mark whose job is to be noticed does not get an
  opacity below 1.
close_reason: A left-edge bar on the warning token, same height as the selection bar, undimmed. A horizontal underline has no edge to sit on in a vertical strip: the next row starts there, so it read as a divider between two tabs rather than a mark on one.

title: The connection row's SSH button is a protocol label pretending to be an action
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Connections.
2. Look at any row in the list.

Expected: it is clear what kind of connection this is, and separately, what
clicking will do.
Actual: one control does both jobs and reads as neither. A button labelled `SSH`
sits at the right of every row; the word names the protocol, the button performs
quick-connect. It looks like a type tag that is somehow pressable.

## Second half: there is no type indicator at all

Every saved profile is SSH today, so nothing has had to say so. That stops being
true the moment a second kind of connection lands, and a list that never said
which was which is a list nobody can read.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The row action is an icon with an accessible name, not the protocol word.
- The protocol is shown as a quiet neutral badge on the row, not as an action.
- The badge stays quiet: it carries no information while SSH is the only kind,
  and must not look as though it does.
- The address ellipses before the badge does when the row is narrow.
close_reason: The row's two jobs are two controls now. Type is a quiet neutral Badge on the meta line, read off Base.type rather than hard-coded, so the first non-SSH profile labels itself instead of silently claiming to be SSH. The action is an IconButton with a Lucide plug glyph and an accessible name, revealed on hover or focus. Two things fell out of it: the neutral tone — the DEFAULT tone, the one you get by writing <Badge> — had no rule at all in badge.css and painted nothing, so it rendered as bare text with padding and read as a stray gap; and the meta line was at 2xs, 10.5px at the current base, which is the bottom of the scale and too small for the only copy of the address.

title: No About section: the app cannot say what version it is
description:
## What is missing

The settings rail has Clipboard, Interface, Export / Backup / Import and
Connections. Nothing says what build this is. A user filing a bug, or checking
whether an update landed, has nothing to read and nothing to quote.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An `About` item in the settings rail showing: version, build date, commit sha,
  the Go and Wails versions it was built with, and the platform.
- The values come from the binary, injected at link time (`-ldflags -X`), not
  from a constant somebody has to remember to bump. A dev build says so rather
  than lying about a version it does not have.
- A new read-only RPC serves them; the frontend does not guess any of it.
- A `Copy diagnostics` button that puts the whole block on the clipboard in one
  action, because the reason anyone opens this page is to paste it into a bug
  report.
- `make build` sets the ldflags, and a test asserts an unset version renders as
  something explicit rather than as an empty row.

title: No way to test an SSH connection without opening a tab
description:
## What is missing

The connection form has Save and nothing else. The only way to find out whether
a profile actually works is to save it, open a tab, and read whatever the shell
prints. That is a slow loop for the exact moment someone is least sure — while
they are typing the credentials in.

## Backend

There is no RPC for this. Measured against `internal/transport/ws.go`: the
method table has `profiles.*`, `groups.*`, `credentials.*`, `settings.*` and
`export.*` — no `ssh.test` and no probe of any kind. So this needs a new method
that dials, completes the handshake and authenticates, then closes without ever
opening a session.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A `Test` button beside Save in the connection form.
- It works on the **unsaved** form — testing before committing a profile is the
  whole point, so it sends the form state, not a profile id.
- Result is shown against the form: reachable / auth failed / host unresolved /
  timed out, with the server error text where there is one.
- A bounded timeout, so a black-holed host cannot hang the button forever, and a
  way to cancel while in flight.
- The button reports the connection outcome only. It never echoes a password, a
  passphrase or a key back to the frontend, in the result or in a log line.
- Go tests cover the four outcomes against the existing SSH test server.

## Depends on

Not blocked by the validation epic, but the two meet in the same button row —
Test on an invalid form should refuse rather than dial.

title: Scroll containers render the engine default scrollbar
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Connections and select a saved profile so the form panel
   overflows.
2. Scroll the form panel.

Expected: a scrollbar that belongs to the app.
Actual: a wide, pale, opaque bar in the engine default treatment, which against
the dark theme reads as a piece of the browser sitting on top of the app. It also
appears without warning, because the panel only overflows once a profile is
selected — so it looks like a stray artefact rather than a scrollbar.

Measured: `grep -rn scrollbar frontend/src/styles` returned nothing. Not one of
the scroll containers was styled — `.cm-form-panel`, `.cm-list`,
`.ui-page__scroll`, `.ui-page__rail`, and the xterm viewport all fell back to the
engine.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Scrollbar thumb and track are drawn from theme tokens, so light and dark are
  correct from one declaration.
- The treatment is declared once at the base layer, not per surface.
- Exactly one mechanism is used. Chromium ignores the `::-webkit-scrollbar`
  pseudo-elements once `scrollbar-width`/`scrollbar-color` are set, so declaring
  both makes WKWebView and Chromium render different scrollbars from the same
  stylesheet.
close_reason: Scrollbar treatment added once at the base layer, thumb and track from theme tokens so light and dark follow without a second declaration. ::-webkit-scrollbar only — Chromium ignores the pseudo-elements once scrollbar-width/scrollbar-color are set, so declaring both would have given WKWebView and Chromium different scrollbars from one stylesheet.

title: The quick-connect action on a connection row is invisible until hover
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Connections.
2. Move the pointer away from the list.

Expected: each row shows that it is connectable.
Actual: the row is two lines of text and nothing else. The "SSH" quick-connect
button (`.cm-item-actions`, `connections.tsx` `renderListItem`) is `opacity: 0`
until `.cm-item:hover`, so a list of fifteen identical rows offers no visible
affordance at all.

## Why hover-reveal is wrong here

Hover-reveal earns its keep when a row carries several actions and showing them
all would be noise. This row carries exactly one. Hiding it buys no quieting and
costs the only signal that a click does something.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The quick-connect button is visible on every connection row without hover.
- No `opacity` transition keyed off `.cm-item:hover` remains in connections.css.
close_reason: Fixed, then deliberately reverted — recorded because the reversal is the finding. Making the button permanent was the wrong answer to a real complaint: the row had nothing that said it was connectable. What was actually wrong is in nocx-fmoz — one control was doing two jobs, naming the protocol and performing an action. Once the row states its own type in a badge, the control no longer has to stay visible to explain the row, so hover-reveal came back. It came back with :focus-within beside :hover, which it never had: an opacity:0 element is still in the tab order, so a keyboard user was tabbing into a button they could not see.

title: The quick-connect palette: fixed size, a real New-connection action, a readable selection
description:
Reported by the owner in one pass. The palette resized as the filter narrowed the list; the
selected row was unreadable because `.item:hover` (class + pseudo-class) outranked
`.item--selected` on background while the label kept the dark text meant for the accent fill — and
`onMouseEnter` sets the selection, so that was every row under the pointer. "New connection" was a
saved profile with an empty host: opening it handed the backend an empty address and the tab came
up on "Terminal failed to start".

## Acceptance Criteria

- The palette keeps one size while filtering, and its empty state occupies the list area rather
  than hanging below it.
- The selected row is legible, including under the pointer.
- A New-connection entry opens Settings on the Connections page with a blank profile, and works
  whether or not Settings was already open.
- Profiles with no host are not offered; a separator appears only between two populated groups.

title: Settings rows: the reset affordance, the modified dot and the storage tag
description:
Three things on one row, each measured on the owner screen.

The reset button sat directly BELOW the control — which is where the pointer already is after
operating that control, so undoing the change just made was one slip away. The modified dot was
rendered only when modified, so its 6px box plus margin entered the flow and shoved the label
sideways the moment a value changed. The storage-class tag (Public/Private/Secret) printed one of
three words on every row with nothing in the product consulting `dataClass` — export eligibility is
decided by the control kind in `Registry.GetSnapshot`, not by the class.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The reset affordance is an icon at the right end of the row, level with the control, in a gutter
  the row reserves whether or not it is showing one.
- The label does not move when a row becomes modified, and its column lines up with the section
  heading above it.
- The storage-class tag is gone from the markup and its CSS with it.
- The rail is one gutter: the filter count and the section counts line up.

title: The vertical strip lists, filters and names its tabs
description:
The vertical placement shipped as a flat list of 38px rows with the strip actions stranded at the
bottom of the column, a horizontal accent bar claiming to be a left-edge one, and the strip itself
sitting left of the activity bar. Warp is the reference for ideas, not a design to copy: the owner
chose search, two-line rows and a left-aligned label, and kept our own left-edge indicator.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The strip sits between the activity bar and the panes.
- Its actions are one group in a header row with the filter field, at the top of the column.
- Typing in the filter hides non-matching rows without closing, deactivating or reordering tabs.
- A row shows the title and, when the title is a NAME rather than the directory, a dimmer second
  line with the cwd or host.
- The label is left-aligned in vertical and still centred in horizontal.
- The active row is marked by the 2px accent bar on its left edge.

title: One base type size, everything else relative to it
description:
Groundwork for the epic: the scale was declared in pixels (12/13/15/18/22) and `body` set
`font-size: var(--font-size-md)`, so the "base" governed nothing — every rule took an absolute
value and there was no single number a zoom control could move. Twenty declarations bypassed the
scale entirely, including a 10px/11px cluster that was one register written as two numbers, and
the terminal DOM at 14px against a canvas at 13.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `--font-size-base` and `--ui-scale` on `:root`, `html` computing `calc(base * scale)`, every
  other type size a rem ratio of it.
- No raw px font-size outside the two documented exceptions (the base anchor and the terminal).
- A lint rule rejects a px font-size TOKEN, with a negative fixture proving it fires.
- The terminal token and `renderers/font.ts::FONT_SIZE` cannot drift apart silently.

title: The activity indicator lights on the tab you just left
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a command in tab 1 and let it print.
2. Switch to tab 2. Tab 1 shows the unread-activity indicator although nothing has happened
   in it since the switch.

## What is happening

`Tab.markActivity()` set the flag for output arriving in the ACTIVE tab, where nothing renders
it, and `setActive()` clears the flag on activation but not on deactivation — so it survived
the switch away. The neighbouring code already had the guard: `updateAgentStatus` checks
`!this._active`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Output arriving in the active tab does not set the unread flag.
- Output arriving in a background tab still does (the existing e2e case passes).

title: Button variants have no rule: two equal actions look different on one page
description:
`Button` offers `default`, `primary`, `danger` and `ghost`, and nothing says when to use which. Counted across the app: default 11, primary 6, danger 3, ghost 1.

On the Export page this is visible in one screen: "Export Configuration" is `default` and "Encrypt and Export" is `primary`, though both are the main action of their own section. The user reads that as two different kinds of button and asks where they came from — they are the same component, chosen differently.

What is missing is written guidance plus enough consistency for it to be believed: one primary per section (the action the section exists for), default for everything secondary, danger for destructive, ghost for a control that is a row rather than a button. Then sweep the call sites.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The rule is written down where a developer will meet it — the kit's README next to Button, and `button.tsx`'s own doc comment.
- Every existing call site matches the rule or carries a comment saying why it does not.
- Two sections of the same kind do not show two different button looks for the same kind of action.
close_reason: Variant rule written where a developer meets it — button.tsx's doc comment and ui/README.md. primary is the one action a section exists for, at most one per section; default for every other real action; danger for destructive; ghost for a control that reads as a row. Two clauses added during review that the first draft did not have: a control that reveals, expands or navigates is not a primary even when it is the only button in its section (which is why Show Backup Paths stayed default), and a button rendered once per row of a list is never primary, because emphasis is spent by repetition. Sweep: Export Configuration, Import and Decrypt and Import to primary; everything on Settings, Connections, Banner and Dialog already matched.

title: Font family and base size become settings
description:
Two independent choices, one mechanism: the UI font (`--font-family-ui`, `--font-size-base`) and the terminal font (`renderers/font.ts`: `FONT_FAMILY`, `FONT_SIZE`, `LINE_HEIGHT`). They are separate on purpose — a terminal wants a monospace at a size the user reads code at; the chrome does not.

The UI half is nearly free now that the scale is relative: one token to write. The terminal half is the work — the renderer must re-measure its cell after a font change and the PTY must be told the new grid, which is the resize path, not a repaint. Changing the family can also change cell width without changing the size, so the two cannot share a code path that assumes only the size moved.

Offer only fonts the host has. Enumerating them is platform work; a documented shortlist with a free-text fallback is an acceptable first cut, and should be named as such.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The UI font family and base size are settings; changing either repaints the chrome live, with no remount and no reload.
- The terminal font family and size are separate settings; changing either re-measures the cell, re-fits the grid and resizes the PTY.
- The relationship between `--font-size-terminal` and `FONT_SIZE` stays enforced (today's unit test) or is replaced by a stronger guarantee.
- A font the host does not have falls back visibly rather than silently rendering in the UA serif — the failure ADR-0013 was written after.

title: UI zoom from the keyboard, driven by --ui-scale
description:
`--ui-scale` exists on `:root` and multiplies `--font-size-base`; nothing writes it yet. Zoom is therefore: a persisted number, three key bindings, and clamping.

Specifics that decide the shape:

- **What zoom covers.** rem-based type scales with the root; the terminal does not (AD-6) and must keep its own size, or the grid and the canvas disagree. Say in the UI what zoom applies to, or the first bug report will be "zoom does not change my terminal".
- **The bindings.** Cmd/Ctrl `+`, `-`, `0` are the convention. They must not reach the PTY — the terminal takes single keystrokes, so this joins the app-hotkey layer, next to Cmd+T and Cmd+,.
- **Persistence.** A settings key, like every other preference, applied live through `SettingsObserver`.
- **Clamping.** Below about 0.8 the 2xs step stops being legible; above about 1.5 the shell chrome starts wrapping. Pick bounds and justify them by looking, not by arithmetic.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Cmd/Ctrl +, − and 0 change and reset the UI scale, and the change is visible without a restart.
- The value persists across a restart and is clamped to documented bounds.
- The terminal's own type does not change with UI zoom, and the UI says so where the user can read it.
- The bindings do not reach the PTY: a test asserts the keystroke does not appear in terminal input.

title: Type is user-adjustable: font, size and zoom
description:
The mechanism landed today and is unused: `tokens.css` declares `--font-size-base` and `--ui-scale` on `:root`, `html` computes `calc(base * scale)`, and every other type size is a rem ratio of it. So UI zoom is now one number, and a size setting is one number — which is exactly why this is worth doing now rather than as five scattered overrides.

The terminal is deliberately NOT on that scale: xterm rasterises from TypeScript (`renderers/font.ts`, `FONT_SIZE`) and does not react to the CSS root, so it needs its own lever and its own live-apply path (AD-6). A unit test already asserts `--font-size-terminal` equals `FONT_SIZE`; whatever ships must keep that true or replace the test with something stronger.

## Success Criteria
See acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: The user can change the UI font family and its base size, change the terminal's font family and size independently, and zoom the whole UI from the keyboard — each persisted across a restart and applied live, without a remount. DONE WHEN all three ship with tests and the type scale still reads zero px font-sizes outside the two documented exceptions. OUT OF SCOPE: per-surface font overrides, font ligature settings, and web-font loading — every font offered is one the host already has.

title: Dragging a tab works with groups — within one and across two
description:
Reordering by drag exists (`onReorder`, wired through TabStripBase). Once the list has groups, a drop is ambiguous: it can mean *move within this group*, *move to another group*, or *nothing, because the group is derived and cannot be assigned*.

That last case is the real question. If groups are derived from `descriptor.surfaceType`, dragging an SSH tab into the "Local" group is a request the model cannot honour — the tab's kind is a fact about its content, not a position. The options are: refuse the drop (and show that it is refused), let the group be an explicit override that the derivation only seeds, or keep drag strictly inside a group. Each is defensible; the task is to pick one and say why.

Also unresolved by the current implementation: the drop indicator. A flat list needs a line between two rows; a grouped list needs to distinguish "between these two rows" from "into this group, at the end".

## Acceptance Criteria

- Dragging a tab to a new position inside its own group reorders it there, and the order survives a strip swap (horizontal ↔ vertical).
- A drag that crosses a group boundary does exactly one documented thing, and a test asserts it — including the case where the answer is a refusal.
- The drop indicator distinguishes a position between rows from a drop onto a group.
- Dragging is unchanged in the horizontal strip.
notes:
RESCOPED 2026-08-01 (.internal/specs/2026-08-01-file-manager-design.md, nocx-gglz): drag BETWEEN groups is removed; drag WITHIN a group stays.

Groups are automatic and keyed by session lineage, so moving a tab across groups is meaningless — a
tab does not change server because it was dragged — and offering it would make the group heading
lie about what is inside it.

title: Tabs group under headings in the vertical strip
description:
Warp sections its tab list with a dim heading per group. We have the natural key already: `descriptor.surfaceType` tells a local terminal from an SSH session from a service surface such as Settings, so nothing new has to be stored to group by it.

The decisions this carries, and why it is not styling:

- **What groups by.** `surfaceType` is the obvious first cut; grouping SSH tabs by host is a second, and the two can disagree. Pick one and write down why.
- **Order.** Tabs are reorderable by drag today. A grouped list either constrains that to within a group or has to re-derive order after every move — the drag half is its own task, so this one must state which it assumes.
- **Filtering.** The strip filters tabs now; a heading whose group is empty after filtering must go with it, or the list reads as broken.
- **The keyboard.** Cmd+1..9 addresses tabs by position; grouping must not change what those keys select.

Groups exist only in the vertical strip. The horizontal one stays a flat row.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Tabs of different kinds render under separate labelled headings in the vertical strip, and the horizontal strip is unchanged.
- A heading disappears when the filter empties its group, and comes back when the filter is cleared.
- Cmd+1..9 selects the same tab it selected before grouping — asserted by a test, not by inspection.
- The grouping key is documented at the code that derives it, with the alternative that was rejected.
notes:
CONSTRAINT added 2026-08-01 (.internal/specs/2026-08-01-file-manager-design.md, nocx-gglz): group identity is session lineage plus the
backend-attested endpoint, NOT the display host.

root@srv-01 and deploy@srv-01 are different filesystems with different permissions; a reconfigured
alias can keep a display host while changing the endpoint. Grouping them under one 'srv-01' heading
would assert something false. This bead now has a second consumer: viewer tabs opened from the file
manager (nocx-708q) join their originating session's group.

title: The vertical tab strip becomes a grouped session list
description:
Warp's tab panel is the reference for ideas, not a design to copy. Search, two-line rows and left-aligned labels shipped separately; what is left are the four items below, each of which carries mechanics rather than styling — which is why they are not one change.

## Success Criteria
See acceptance. Each child lands with its own tests and leaves the CSS integrity gate at zero.
acceptance_criteria: The vertical strip lists tabs in labelled groups; a tab can be dragged within its group and between groups; each row carries a glyph naming what kind of session it is; and the strip's width is draggable and survives a restart. DONE WHEN all four ship with tests and the strip still passes the kit gates. OUT OF SCOPE: any change to the horizontal strip, the round avatar Warp draws for agent sessions, and tab search (shipped separately).

title: dev-web's WS port collides with the e2e headless runbook
description:
## Description

`make dev-web` pins `NOCX_WS_PORT=9876`, which is the same port the headless e2e
path pins for devharness (`.internal/briefs/w6-devharness-verify.md`,
`.internal/reports/devharness-verify.md`). A look-and-see session and a test run
evict each other on the backend socket the same way they used to on 5173 — the
web port was moved to 5180 for exactly that reason and the WS port was left
behind.

`frontend/vite.dev-view.config.ts` is worse: its `NOCX_WEB_PORT` fallback is
`5173` outright, so running the config without the script lands straight on the
e2e/dev vite port.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the headless e2e backend: `NOCX_WS_ADDR=127.0.0.1:9876 go run ./cmd/devharness`
2. In another shell: `make dev-web`
3. It refuses to start — `port 9876 (backend WS) is already in use`. Reverse the
   order and the e2e run is the one that loses.
4. Separately: `cd frontend && npx vite --config vite.dev-view.config.ts` with no
   env — vite binds 5173, the e2e/dev port.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `make dev-web` defaults to a WS/web pair no other consumer claims, and both
  sit below the Linux ephemeral range (32768-60999) so `wails dev`s
  `127.0.0.1:0` backend cannot land on them either.
- `vite.dev-view.config.ts` fallbacks match the script rather than 5173/9876.
- The Makefile and script comments name the full port map, not just 5173.
close_reason: dev-web now owns 5180/9880; both fallbacks in vite.dev-view.config.ts match the script. Verified live: backend 127.0.0.1:9880, vite 127.0.0.1:5180, shim reports GetWSPort()===9880, a pre-existing 5173 server untouched. Commit a637649 on fix/dev-web-ports-nocx-z069.

title: The type scale has no small end, and the DOM's terminal text is 1px larger than the terminal
description:
Rule 7 (T20, nocx-zhjx) ships with an exemption list because the remaining 18 px font-sizes are two decisions rather than 18 mistakes, and neither can be made by arithmetic.

**The small end of the scale.** The scale is 12/13/15/18/22 (--font-size-xs..xl). Eight declarations use 11px and four use 10px: the tab index pill, the tab bar and vertical strip, the command editor's chrome, a Button at data-size=sm, the settings error, the export backup details, the Badge, the settings badge and breadcrumb, and the update notice. That is a register the scale does not have — 'smaller than xs' — not a dozen slips. Collapsing them into 12px is a visual change in twelve places, and this epic has twice been bitten by CSS that was obviously equivalent and was not. Decide it on a running page: either add the missing step, or move each to the nearest token having looked at it.

**The terminal register is inconsistent with the terminal.** frontend/src/renderers/font.ts sets FONT_SIZE = 13, so xterm draws the live screen at 13px. The DOM that shows the same content — .cmd-output, .term-line, .cmd-header-text and .nocx-editor-input — is 14px. A command block therefore changes size depending on whether it is being drawn by the canvas or by the DOM, which is a defect independent of tokens. --font-size-sm is already 13px, so the fix may be a one-token substitution; it needs looking at, because the mono metrics differ from the UI font's at the same nominal size.

Not in scope: 16px on .ui-icon-button[data-size='sm'], which is a glyph box for a '×' rather than type. If it moves it should become an icon-size declaration, not a font-size token.
acceptance_criteria: Every px font-size outside the token layer is either replaced by a token or deliberately kept with the decision recorded; rule 7's exemption list shrinks to what survives that decision; the mono blocks and the xterm canvas agree on a size or the difference is deliberate and stated.
notes: shipped: added --font-size-2xs (0.75rem) for the small-end register (replaced all 10px/11px); converted scale from px to rem with --font-size-base: 15px and --ui-scale: 1 for zoom; added --font-size-terminal: 13px matching FONT_SIZE; fixed terminal DOM 14px → terminal token; converted icon-button sm from font-size: 16px to SVG sizing; added unit test + CSS integrity rule enforcing px tokens are relative (except base and terminal); emptied all 19 rule-7 exemptions

title: Focus placement after a page switch belongs to Page, not to settings.tsx
description:
Reported by the T19 worker (nocx-dli6) in a correction to its own worker_done — it named this gap rather than letting it pass, which is worth recording.

Spec §3.8 lists focus placement after a page change among Page's duties. It works today, and the proof matrix's two 'focus placement after page switch' cases pass — but the behaviour lives in settings.tsx's handleKeydown, which also owns slash-to-search and Escape-to-clear. So this is misplaced ownership rather than missing behaviour: any future Page gets the rail, the scroll mode and the header for free, and would have to reimplement focus placement.

Not blocking. The matrix covers the behaviour, so a move can be verified rather than guessed at.
acceptance_criteria: Page places focus after a page change; settings.tsx's handleKeydown owns only domain behaviour, and the proof matrix's Page-duties cases still pass
close_reason: Page owns focus placement after a page change, keyed on title; the surface keeps deep-link focus, which is domain behaviour

title: Commit messages must name their bead
description:
Requested by the owner 2026-07-28. Every commit message carries the bead id of the work it does, in a standardised format documented under Git authority in AGENTS.md.

Enforced by eye at review for now. If that stops working, the follow-up is a commit-msg hook rejecting a subject with no (nocx-...) — file it rather than letting the convention rot.
acceptance_criteria: AGENTS.md states the commit format including the bead id, and the rule is being followed on new commits
close_reason: Format documented under Git authority in AGENTS.md

title: make dev-web: the browser dev stand as one command
description:
Look-and-see loop in an ordinary browser over an SSH tunnel: cmd/devharness plus vite with the two Wails bindings shimmed, ports read off the backend's stdout instead of copied by hand.

Port 5180, kept off 5173 because the headless e2e path serves the frontend there (playwright.config.ts BASE_URL).

Preflight check on both ports: a leftover vite on [::1]:5173 and a fresh one on 127.0.0.1:5173 do not collide at bind time, so localhost (::1 first here) reached the un-shimmed page and the WS was refused for an empty token.
acceptance_criteria: `make dev-web` starts backend + frontend, prints the ssh -L line, and a browser at the printed URL reaches an app whose WebSocket connects; a busy port fails loudly naming the holder instead of serving an un-shimmed page.
close_reason: Landed: Makefile dev-web target + scripts/dev-web.sh + frontend/vite.dev-view.config.ts (made permanent). Port 5180 rather than 5173 because the headless e2e path serves the frontend on 5173 (playwright.config.ts BASE_URL) — sharing it means a test run and a look-and-see session evict each other, or one attaches to the other's server via PW_REUSE_SERVER and reports on a tree it never built. Preflight port check because vite strictPort does not cover it: a vite on [::1]:5173 and one on 127.0.0.1:5173 both bind fine and neither notices the other, and since localhost resolves ::1 first here the browser reached the un-shimmed page — the only symptom being a WebSocket refused for an empty token. Same reason the printed ssh -L line spells the remote side 127.0.0.1. Verified in headless chromium: WS open to /session, no close, renderer mounted 80x24.

title: IconButton owns the selected indicator the activity bar draws for it
description:
Split out of nocx-zeti. The rule-3 decision allows a parent to reference a kit identity
for PLACEMENT only, which resolves eleven of the twelve cases found while landing
IconButton (nocx-wqrq) and Toolbar (nocx-jdhy).

The twelfth is genuinely appearance: `.activity-bar .ui-icon-button[aria-selected='true']::before`
draws the active-view indicator bar. A pseudo-element that paints is not placement under
any reading, so the surface must stop owning it.

It belongs to IconButton as a variant — the primitive already takes a `selected` prop, so
the indicator is a presentation of a state it already knows about.

Blocks T20 (nocx-zhjx), where rule 3 is enabled: leaving this in place forces either a
rule with a hole in it or an exemption on its first day.
acceptance_criteria: No surface selector declares appearance on a kit identity; the activity bar's selected indicator is an IconButton variant and its ::before is gone from style.css
close_reason: railIndicator prop; ::before moved into icon-button.css with position:relative in the base; surface reduced to placement

title: deleteProfile swallows RPC failures silently
description:
`connections.tsx` catches and discards the error: `catch { // Silent fail }`. Deletion works today, so the defect is invisible — until the RPC fails, at which point the row stays on screen, no message appears, and the user has no way to tell whether anything happened.

A catch that exists only to silence is worse than no catch: the failure still occurs, and now nothing records it.
close_reason: Already fixed on main and not closed. The bead describes 'catch { // Silent fail }' in connections.tsx; no such code remains (grep over frontend/src finds neither 'Silent fail' nor an empty catch), and the sole caller, connections.tsx:333-349, logs and raises a danger toast: 'Could not delete "<name>": <message>'. Verified 2026-07-29 while scoping the connection-manager redesign (nocx-52cd).

title: The tab index pill and the activity dot express one state twice, and collide
description:
Seen on 2026-07-27. The index pill renders only on the active tab, and the activity dot overlaps the number where both are present.

This is a design question before it is a CSS fix, and the fix should not start until it is answered: decide what the number carries and what the dot carries. If the number is a keyboard-shortcut affordance it belongs on every tab; if the dot means unseen output it is meaningless on the tab you are looking at. Today they say overlapping things in the same 16 pixels.

title: T18: quick-connect, banners and update-notice
description: Spec §6.2. QuickConnectRow stays with quick-connect — a generic ListRow arrives only when a second consumer does. Done when no surface selector addresses a kit identity; enables rules 3 and 10.
close_reason: No appearance left in these surfaces to move; deleted the dead .clipboard-banner-* rules the earlier transactions left behind

title: T16: retire the documents describing the old contract
description: Spec §6.2. ui/README.md:106 and dialog.tsx:124,172 describe a scope that no longer exists. Rule 6 permits them; leaving them is how the next agent rebuilds what was just removed.
close_reason: README rewritten to identities; kit.css references and the redundant Toggle section removed; dialog.tsx cleaned by T15

title: T13: Toolbar — structural, class bounded to layout
description: Spec §3.6. Same contract as Field. Consider the start/end slot composition as the replacement for placement classes.
close_reason: border-bottom moved from the surface into toolbar.css; placement stays with the surface

title: T10: EmptyState owns its element
description: Spec §3.6. Already emits ui-empty-state; loses its class prop and gains its identity test.
close_reason: class prop removed, dead .cm-list-empty rule deleted, passthrough test replaced by an identity test

title: T12: Section — structural, class bounded to layout
description: Spec §3.6. Same contract as Field.
close_reason: Two hand-rolled section divs became Sections; heading treatment and row gap folded into section.css; identity order pinned

title: T11: Field — structural, class bounded to layout
description: Spec §3.6. class stays but may carry only layout and placement — never background, border, radius, color, font, padding, shadow, appearance or a drawing pseudo-element. Rule 11's traced-class tier enforces it.
close_reason: class prop removed outright — zero consumers; identity pinned for both orientations

title: T9: Badge owns its element
description: Spec §3.6. Gains a ui-badge base class; the variant classes become tone: neutral | info | warning | danger.
close_reason: ui-badge base + data-tone; badge.css collapsed to one base and three overrides

title: [epic] A catalogue of terminal palettes, not two themes
description:
nocx ships two themes. Users coming from Warp, iTerm or Tabby expect a catalogue,
and ADR-0013 already makes this cheap: `--terminal-*` (background, foreground,
cursor, selection, ANSI 0-15) lives in the theme file, and `theme-adapter.ts`
reads it out of computed style. A terminal palette is therefore a data row, not
a code change.

Two MIT-licensed sources are already on this machine and were read while
investigating this:

- `~/repos/orca/src/renderer/src/lib/terminal-themes/` — 9 files
  (classic, popular-dark, popular-dark-core, popular-dark-extended,
  popular-light, defaults) of xterm `ITheme` objects, exactly our
  `--terminal-*` shape. MIT, Copyright (c) 2026 Lovecast Inc.
- `~/repos/orca/src/main/warp-themes/` — a parser for Warp's own theme files,
  so a user's existing Warp themes could be imported rather than re-typed.

What neither source provides, and what must not be confused with this: a **UI**
palette. Orca's chrome is one shadcn light/dark pair; Tabby's is Bootstrap
variables over a single dark background. Our `--color-*` tokens — canvas,
chrome, surface, border, text — have no counterpart to copy, and the contrast
work in nocx-u7wq was done by measurement for that reason.

So the shape of this is: a terminal-palette catalogue, with each entry providing
`--terminal-*` only, paired with one of the two UI palettes (light or dark)
chosen by the entry's own background luminance. Attribution required — MIT
notice for whatever is lifted.

## Success Criteria

A user can choose from at least a dozen named terminal palettes in Settings, the
choice repaints open terminals in place without a restart, and each palette
declares whether it pairs with the light or the dark UI. Adding the next palette
is one data entry and no code. Third-party MIT notices are recorded.

Out of scope: importing Warp/iTerm theme files from disk (a follow-on), and any
change to the UI colour tokens.

title: Ten colour literals hide in var() fallbacks and inline styles
description: Found by nocx-xrrl.4, which is the first independent check of the token migration's claim. Both shapes are invisible to a grep over CSS files: var(--x, #hex) hides a literal inside a fallback, and a JSX style prop is not in a stylesheet at all. That is precisely why ADR-0013 section 4 asked for a grammar rather than a denylist, and the check earned its keep on day one.
acceptance_criteria: The colour-literals baseline is empty: the six var() fallbacks in overlay.css either drop their fallback or use a token, and the four inline style colours in connections.tsx move to CSS classes. nocx-xrrl cannot close while the baseline is non-empty.
close_reason: Closed by nocx-vxqj.9: the six var() fallbacks in overlay.css and the four inline style colours in connections.tsx are gone; the colour-literals baseline is empty.

title: Eight raw controls survive in already-migrated shell surfaces
description:
Found when the guard's baseline was regenerated. banner (3), sidebar (2), tab-strip (2) and update-notice (1) all went through the Solid migration this session and still use raw <button>. They are not sloppiness: a tab close button and an activity-bar icon button are chrome-sized, and the kit's Button carries padding and variants built for form actions. Adopting it would restyle the shell.

This is the same shape as the Field problem (nocx-vxqj.7): a kit component built for one kind of consumer does not fit another, and the surface keeps its own. Worth deciding once for both.
